chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: Executive Summary of the 2025 American Thyroid Association Management Guidelines for Adult Patients with Differentiated Thyroid Cancer Stephanie Smooke Praw, 1 Benjamin J. Gigliotti, 2 Alex Tessnow,3 Hyunseok Kang,4 and Debra J. Margulies 5 Background: Developed by members of the American Thyroid Association (ATA) Clinical Affairs Committee, this executive summary of the 2025 ATA guidelines for adult patients with differentiated thyroid cancer provides a summary of key points and recommendations with an emphasis on notable differences between the 2025 and 2015 guidelines. Summary: The updated guidelines emphasize individualized care through the DATA framework (Diagnosis, risk/beneﬁt Assessment, Treatment decisions, and response Assessment) with the goal of enhancing shared decision-making and personalized care. Highlights include expanded role of molecular diagnostics, re ﬁned risk stratiﬁcation, greater emphasis on active surveillance and lobectomy, inclusion of ablative procedures, and selec- tive use of external beam radiation therapy and chemoradiotherapy. De-escalation of surveillance for low-risk patients and introduction of the concept of complete remission are also new.

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: Conclusions: This executive summary aims to provide a summary of key points and recommendations with an emphasis on notable differences between the 2025 and 2015 guidelines. Keywords: American Thyroid Association (ATA) guidelines, differentiated thyroid cancer, pathology- thyroid, surgery-adult thyroid Introduction and Rationale S ince the publication of the 2015 American Thyroid Association (ATA) guidelines, there have been changes in the epidemiology, classi ﬁcation, and management of dif- ferentiated thyroid cancer (DTC). 1 The updated 2025 guide- lines are informed by a decrease in the incidence of DTC, insights into thyroid cancer genomics, expanded molecular diagnostics, enhanced management options for advanced thyroid cancer, and increased emphasis on shared decision- making with the goal of creating a personalized treatment approach.2 The 2025 guidelines employ a new approach to clinical decision-making, referred to as DATA-Diagnosis, risk/beneﬁt Assessment, Treatment decisions, and response Assessment. Interventions are assessed using individual patient factors to determine whether a particular intervention is appropriate.

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: This approach facilitates shared decision-making when multiple management strategies are available. Following intervention, the 2025 ATA risk assessment tool should be used to evaluate response and guide decisions regarding ongoing monitoring and/or additional treatment, from ini- tial diagnosis through survivorship. The 2025 guidelines also include several Good Practice Statements as alternatives to graded recommendations when the quality of evidence is low or insuf ﬁcient. These are intended to be strong recommendations applicable to nearly all persons or situations and required unanimous consensus from the guideline group. The Clinical Affairs Committee of the ATA has devel- oped this executive summary of the 2025 ATA guidelines on DTC to provide a summary of key points and recommenda- tions with an emphasis on notable differences between the 2025 and 2015 guidelines. Recommendation (R) numbers, ﬁgures, and tables referenced throughout correlate directly with the 2025 ATA guideline document. 1Division of Endocrinology, Diabetes, and Metabolism, Department of Medicine, University of California Los Angeles David Geffen School of Medicine, Los Angeles, California, USA.

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: Key New Recommendations/Key Changes Initial management of DTC There are several new and updated recommendations regarding the preoperative management of DTC ( Table 1). It is now explicitly recommended that thyroid cancer surgery be performed by a high-volume surgeon ( ‡25 thyroidecto- mies/year) (R6). Preoperative neck ultrasound to evaluate for the presence of invasion of tumor into surrounding struc- tures and for cervical lymphadenopathy is also strongly rec- ommended (R7). Fine needle aspiration with thyroglobulin (Tg) needle washout is again advised for lymph nodes with a short axis of ‡8 mm, if this would impact surgical manage- ment (R7). CT or MRI of the neck and mediastinum with intravenous contrast is recommended if there is bulky lymph node involvement or suspicion of invasion of the aerodiges- tive tract or mediastinum. PET/CT is not recommended rou- tinely (R8). Molecular diagnostic studies may be considered in surgical planning when available or performed, but rou- tine use is not recommended (R10). For T1a tumors, greater emphasis is placed on active sur- veillance, which yields oncologic and quality of life outcomes comparable with immediate surgery (R11-14).

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: Ultrasound should be performed every 6 months for 1 –2 years, then annually by an experienced sonographer. Surgery is recom- mended if there is evidence of progression or per patient pref- erence. The use of percutaneous ablation of T1a disease as an alternative method to surgery, in select patients, after discus- sion of risks and beneﬁts, is new (R11). The role of lobectomy has been expanded, given that recur- rence rates are comparable with thyroidectomy, but with fewer complications and less need for thyroid hormone supplemen- tation (R15). Tumors <2 cm without extrathyroidal extension (ETE) or suspicious lymph nodes should be managed with lobectomy unless contraindicated (e.g., contralateral nodules). Lobectomy may also be appropriate for 2 –4 cm tumors, if there are no contralateral nodules or ETE. For tumors >4c m , or those with ETE or nodal disease, total thyroidectomy with lymph node dissection remains recommended. The 2025 guidelines recognize that central neck dissection (CLND) increases the risk of complications. Prophylactic CLND (pCLND) for cN0 disease does not improve long- term outcomes in T1 –T2 tumors and is now more strongly discouraged (R19).

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: For larger cN0 tumors, pCLND may be considered, though evidence is limited and risks must be weighed. Importantly, ipsilateral CLND is recommended when lateral neck nodal disease is present (R20). Therapeu- tic CLND should be performed if nodal involvement is sus- pected preoperatively. Abnormal central nodes (cN1a) on imaging warrant CLND to achieve maximal resection. Intraoperative nerve monitoring of the recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) and external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve may be performed during surgery to improve postoper- ative voice outcomes (R23). The 2025 guidelines also newly advise considering RLN status when deciding on completion thyroidectomy (R16). New postoperative recommendations include calcium and vitamin D supplementation or selective use based on rapid postoperative parathyroid hormone testing following total or completion thyroidectomy (R24), avoidance of routine surgi- cal drains (R25), and early referral for RLN injury to a speech language pathologist or voice-specialized physician (R26). Genetic considerations have also been expanded.

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: While the 2015 guidelines noted syndromic DTC, the 2025 update conditionally recommends careful history and physical exam, while ultrasound screening may be performed for familial nonmedullary thyroid cancer when three or more ﬁrst or second-degree family members are affected (R2-5). Initial postoperative management of DTC Updates in histopathologic evaluation re ﬂect the latest World Health Organization classiﬁcation of thyroid tumors to ensure accurate reporting (R27). 3 Key changes include: renaming encapsulated follicular variant of papillary thyroid cancer (IEFVPTC) without invasion as noninvasive follicular thyroid neoplasm with papillary-like nuclear features, now classiﬁed as a low-risk neoplasm not requiring completion surgery or RAI; designating IEFVPTC with minimal capsular invasion as a “favorable outcome ” variant; and identifying oncocytic thyroid carcinoma (OTC) and high-grade follicular cell—derived nonanaplastic thyroid carcinoma as distinct subtypes associated with unfavorable outcomes.

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: The 2025 ATA Risk Strati ﬁcation System incorporates updated American Joint Committee on Cancer staging, results of molecular pro ﬁling if available or performed, and postoperative imaging and serum Tg and TgAb testing, when appropriate, to estimate risk of persistence/recurrence and survival (R28). 4 The 2025 guidelines maintain the same ATA Response Criteria categories —excellent, indetermi- nate, biochemically incomplete, and structurally incomplete (R29). There are revised Tg thresholds and clearer guidance on applying response criteria to patients following hemithy- roidectomy or thyroidectomy without radioactive iodine (RAI). An updated postoperative risk of recurrence (ROR) stratiﬁca- tion system is provided, incorporating additional features found to in ﬂuence overall risk and re ﬁning others (Fig. 2 of 2025 ATA Guidelines). The 3-tiered system from 2015 is now a 4-tier system including low, low-intermediate, intermediate- high, and high ROR categories. Additionally, separate ROR descriptions are provided for papillary thyroid cancer, follicular thyroid cancer (FTC)/IEFVPTC, and OTC.

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: Notable updates include distinguishing N1a as lower risk than N1b disease, assigning a higher ROR for multifocal disease (even for T1 tumors), reclassifying microscopic ETE as a lower-risk feature than previously recognized, and differentiating microscopically positive posterior margins as higher risk than anterior. Notably, BRAF and TERT mutations have been removed from the picto- rial depiction of estimated structural recurrence risk. The 2025 guidelines include a formal recommendation on the utility of molecular proﬁl i n gt of u r t h e rr eﬁne recurrence risk if available. Limited vascular invasion ( <4 vessels) in OTC and FTC/ IEFVPTC is now categorized as low-intermediate risk (10%– 15% ROR), whereas in 2015 this was described as a low-risk feature (2%–3% ROR). Additionally, the high-risk category is expanded to include poorly differentiated thyroid cancer (PDTC), high-grade cancers, and extranodal extension. When estimating ROR, the 2025 guidelines recommend measuring Tg and TgAb 6 –12 weeks after surgery rather than 3–4 weeks, re ﬂecting updated data on postoperative Tg nadir kinetics (R30).

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: Table 1. Notable Changes in Management of DTC Topic 2015 ATA recommendations 2025 ATA recommendations NIFTP (R1) None New pathological distinction Germline genetic testing (R2–5) Discussed without speci ﬁc recommendations Germline genetic testing may be of bene ﬁt in syndromic familial non- medullary cases. Screening for DICER1 in some instances. Consider neck ultrasound for those with >3 ﬁrst or second degree family members with DTC. High volume surgeon (R6) Discussed in text only Thyroid cancer cases should be referred to high-volume surgeons (>25–50 cases/year). Initial preoperative management (R7–10) Pre-op neck ultrasound to evaluate LNs with biopsy and possible Tg washout. Cross-sectional imaging with CT or MRI for clinical suspicion of advanced disease. Routine Tg not recommended. Preoperative imaging should also assess for presence of gross extra- thyroidal extension and aero-digestive extent. GPS for chest and abdominal imaging if would affect the extent of surgery. Active surveillance (R11–14) Microcarcinomas and patients with high surgical risk can be managed with active surveillance Added percutaneous ablation as an alternative in select patients.

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: Shared decision-making with patients is essential. For those undergoing AS, monitoring with ultrasound advised and measurement of Tg/TgAb is recommended. Surgery if signs of progression. Surgical management (R15–16) Lobectomy preferred for tumors <1c m .F o rt u m o r s 1–4 cm either lobectomy or total thyroidectomy Updated to lobectomy preferred for tumors <2c ma n df o r2–4c m , either lobe or total may be warranted. RLN status should be considered in decision of completion thyroidectomy. Thyroglossal duct associated cancer (R17–18) None Sistrunk procedure recommended along with thyroidectomy if large tumor, evidence of extension outside duct or clinical node involvement. Lymph node management (R19–20) Surgery without proph CND is appropriate for T1/T2 tumors with no clinical node involvement. CND should be considered in N1b cases. Proph CND should not be performed for clinical node-negative T1/T2 tumors. Ipsilateral proph CND is recommended if N1b disease. Voice/Nerve monitoring (R21–23) Visualization of RLN should be performed. Intraoperative RLN nerve monitoring may be considered.

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: In addition to visual ID, RLN monitoring and visual ID and monitoring of external branch of SLN may be performed. Intraoperative vagal or RLN stimulation should be performed prior to removing contralateral lobe. Parathyroid/Calcium (R24) Parathyroids should be seen and preserved In addition, parathyroids removed should be reimplanted. Start calcium/vit D if total or completion thyroidectomy. Surgical drain (R25) None Surgical drains not routinely recommended. Postoperative voice (R26) Postoperative voice should be assessed. Laryngeal exam if abnormal Addition of GPS for timely referral to voice specialist if known RLN injury. Histopathology (R27) Tumor classi ﬁcation based on 2015 WHO; NIFTP considered malignant (encapsulated FVPTC) and OTC entitled HCC and a subtype of FTC WHO updates incorporated: NIFTP reclassiﬁed as non-malignant; IEFVPTC with minimal invasion recognized and designated as having “favorable outcome”; OTC and High-grade follicular-derived non-anaplastic thyroid carcinoma recognized and classiﬁed as having “unfavorable outcome.” (continued) 1216

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: Table 1. (Continued) Topic 2015 ATA recommendations 2025 ATA recommendations Risk Stratiﬁcation and response (R28–R30) 3-tier ROR system; Tg/TgAb at 3 –4 weeks post-op; Tg cutoffs mainly for thyroidectomy + RAI 4-tier ROR system with re ﬁned features and inclusion of new; integrates AJCC 8th ed. and WHO updates; Tg/TgAb at 6 –12 weeks; Tg cutoffs now also for total thyroidectomy without RAI (<2.5 ng/mL). Imaging and FNA immediately following initial surgery (R31) Limited discussion More speci ﬁc guidance: US/cross-sectional imaging before RAI if not “excellent response” or +TgAb; US preferred; cross-sectional imaging (lung/bone) if US inconclusive; PET/CT again recommended for OTC/PDTC with persistent disease concern Radioactive iodine (R32–43) Role tied to ROR categories; rhTSH alternative to withdrawal; pregnancy avoidance 6–12 months More individualized RAI use (esp. low-intermediate / intermediate-high risk); nuanced dosing by ROR tier; OTC —limited outcomes data for RAI; rhTSH now preferred even in high-risk; expanded counseling (SPMs, salivary/lacrimal side effects); pregnancy avoidance ‡6 months; reassure female patients on fertility.

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: Radiotherapy +/- chemotherapy (R44) Recommended against for initial postoperative management EBRT recommended post-surgery for select high-risk patients where progression unlikely salvageable; EBRT/chemo for gross residual or unresectable locally advanced disease. TSH suppression (R45-46) Numeric TSH targets: “Low normal” 0.5–2.0 mU/L, 0.1–0.5 mU/L, and <0.1 mU/L. Binary TSH targets: “within normal reference range” and “below normal reference range.” Serum Tg (R47) Tg assays should be calibrated; Tg should be monitored at a frequency commiserate with risk Additions: Trending Tg after lobectomy not routinely recommended; TgAb trends may be helpful, but imaging surveillance should be primary. De-escalation/discontinuation of monitoring (R48) None Stop US surveillance after 5 –8 years, and Tg monitoring after 10 – 15 years (due to “complete response”) is reasonable in low-risk DTC s/p total thyroidectomy with an excellent response; monitor US q1- 3 years for 5 years after lobectomy if no nodules, or use nodule guidelines if nodules are present.

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: Role of iodine WBS and PET/CT (R49, R50) Diagnostic WBS can be done 6 –12 months after RAI therapy, SPECT/CT is preferred over planar imaging for RAI localization Diagnostic WBS does not need to be routinely done, and is not recommended after lobectomy or thyroidectomy without RAI; SPECT-CT + planar imaging can help localize RAI uptake. Ongoing risk stratiﬁcation (R51) Ongoing risk-strati ﬁcation (response to therapy) is mentioned in main text Ongoing risk-stratiﬁcation (response to therapy) is an explicitly recommended strategy.

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: Rx of locoregional residual, recurrent, or progressive DTC (R52–54) Re-operation thresholds for cervical nodes: Central neck ‡8m mo rl a t e r a ln e c k‡10 mm (short axis); RAI and EBRT mentioned in main text Re-operation thresholds should include size, location, pace, patient factors and preferences, and big picture goals; RAI and EBRT given their own recommendations for use RAI for locoregional and/or distant mets (R55–57) Avoid >5.5 GBq/150 mCi if age >70 years; insufﬁcient data to recommend dosimetry; insuf ﬁcient evidence for rhTSH—consider in select populations Avoid >5.5 GBq/150 mC if age >70 years or renal insuf ﬁciency; use dosimetry if needed, consider its use in other cases; rhTSH or LT4 withdrawal are appropriate.

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: Empirical RAI for Tg positive, imaging negative DTC (R58) TSH suppression and surveillance for indeterminate response; empirical RAI if Tg high or rising; okay to repeat if persistent but responding No signiﬁcant changes RAI refractory DTC (R59) RAIR-DTC is classi ﬁed via 4 criteria; avoid further I-131 if present Do not diagnose RAIR-DTC unless status post at least an ablative dose of I-131, consider I-131 response as a spectrum and use criteria to gauge likelihood of response. (continued) 1217

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: Table 1. (Continued) Topic 2015 ATA recommendations 2025 ATA recommendations General principles of management of RAIR DTC (R60 –61) BRAF or other mutational testing is not routinely recommended for prognostic purpose Molecular proﬁling not routinely recommended in absence of planned systemic therapy, but tissue-based biomarker testing should be performed prior to initiating systemic therapy. Initial Treatment of RAIR DTC (R62–71) MKI therapy should be considered for progressive RAIR DTC MKI therapy is strongly recommended for progressive RAIR DTC without biomarker-linked FDA-approved therapy and lenvatinib is preferred agent. The starting dose of 24 mg for Lenvatinib is recommended for most patients and they should be monitored in a speci ﬁc interval. Cabozantinib as 2nd line after lenvatinib in absence of speci ﬁc biomarker. Speciﬁc targeted therapies for NTRK, RET, ALK and BRAF V600E should be used for patients with corresponding biomarkers.

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: Management of progressive RAIR DTC after initial therapy (R72–77) Molecular testing is limited for research purposes Redifferentiation therapy needs further research Molecular testing is recommended for progressive disease to identify mechanisms of resistance. Redifferentiation therapy for select patients. Immune checkpoint inhibitor is recommended for TMB-high or MMR deﬁcient RAIR DTC. Recommendation for local therapy for solitary or oligometastatic disease. Special considerations (R78-80) Bone-modifying agents are recommended for patients with bone metastases Highlights careful modiﬁcation of dosing schedule for patients at risk for osteonecrosis of jaw Management of Pregnant patients with DTC (R81) Management of pregnant patients with DTC was incorporated with approaches to patients with malignant or indeterminant cytology from FNA A new recommendation that applies to pregnant patients with DTC—states surgery can be delayed until delivery in most patients. US monitoring at least once in early 2nd trimester. TSH goals, monitoring with US and Tg for incomplete response should remain the same as determined preconception.

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: recommended for patients after total thyroidectomy who do not receive RAI; < 2.5 ng/mL de ﬁnes an “excellent” response, 2.5–5 ng/mL de ﬁnes an “indeterminate” response, and >5n g / m Ld eﬁnes a “biochemically incomplete” response (Table 9 of 2025 ATA Guidelines). More speciﬁc recommendations for postoperative imaging before radioactive iodine (RAI) are provided (R31). PET/CT is recommended for patients with OTC or PDTC when there is concern for persistent disease, typically indicated by ele- vated serum Tg and/or TgAb and negative or inconclusive ultrasound. Ultrasound before RAI is recommended for patients who do not have an “excellent” response or have elevated TgAb. Lung and bone cross-sectional imaging is recommended if ultrasound is inconclusive. The role of RAI remains largely unchanged, but greater ﬂexibility is allowed for individualized decisions in patients with “low-intermediate” and “intermediate-high ” risk dis- ease, with increased emphasis on pretreatment counseling.

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: Other notable changes include more nuanced recommenda- tions for each ROR tier ( Table 1 ), a new recommendation highlighting limited outcomes data for use of RAI in OTC and preference for use of recombinant human thyrotropin (rhTSH) over thyroid hormone withdrawal. More attention is also paid to counseling on radiation safety and RAI risks, including second primary malignancy and salivary gland and lacrimal duct complications. Conception avoidance is now recommended for ‡6 months (rather than 6 –12) and female patients can be counseled that RAI does not impact fertility at typical administered doses. The 2025 guidelines permit selective use of external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) after initial surgery, particularly for patients with high-risk features for locoregional progression, especially if not expected to be amenable to salvage surgery. EBRT can now be considered for patients with gross residual disease or locally advanced, unresectable disease where improved locoregional control is anticipated with treatment. The option of concurrent chemotherapy is also newly recom- mended.

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: Counseling regarding potential toxicity and impact on survival of these interventions is emphasized (R44). Long-term management of DTC Several changes are recommended for the long-term man- agement of DTC patients, including new TSH targets (R45), de-escalation of surveillance in low-risk patients (R48), intro- duction of the term “complete remission “(R48), and recom- mendations for appropriate use of percutaneous ethanol and radiofrequency ablation (RFA) for recurrences (R52). The approach to TSH suppression has been simpli ﬁed into a binary system. Table 9 of the 2025 ATA Guidelines sum- marizes TSH targets based on the ATA Response Criteria during ongoing reassessment. TSH goals are strati ﬁed to “within normal reference range” versus “below normal refer- ence range” due to inconclusive or conﬂicting data on speciﬁc numeric targets. The TSH target after total thyroidectomy with or without RAI is now “within normal reference range ” for an excellent or indeterminate response and “below normal reference range ” for a biochemically or structurally incom- plete response. There are only two response criteria after hemithyroidectomy: excellent and structurally incomplete response.

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: Maintaining TSH suppression for up to 5 years in high-risk patients with excellent or indeterminate response to therapy is no longer explicitly recommended. Recommendations for Tg measurement are similar to 2015, with the addition of a speci ﬁc recommendation regarding the limitations of Tg monitoring after hemithyroidectomy; a one- time measurement is recommended as potentially helpful to ensure it is not unexpectedly elevated, although a speciﬁc cut- off is not given. Trending TgAb as a surrogate tumor marker is discussed, although imaging is still recommended as the pri- mary surveillance modality if TgAb levels are positive (R47). Recognizing the long-term burden of surveillance, de- escalation over time is newly given its own recommendation (R48 and Table 11 of the 2025 ATA Guidelines). Patients with a low risk of recurrence and a persistent “excellent” response after total thyroidectomy, with or without RAI (nega- tive imaging, Tg <0.2 ng/mL after RAI or <2.5 ng/mL without RAI), can discontinue ultrasound surveillance after 5–8 years in favor of every 1 –2-year Tg monitoring.

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: After 10 –15 years of ongoing “excellent” response, patients are newly consid- ered to have entered “complete remission,” and biochemical monitoring can also be discontinued. Offering the option to discontinue both biochemical and radiographical surveillance is a major paradigm shift, bringing management of low-risk D T Ci n t oc l o s e rp a r i t yw i t ht h el a r g e rﬁeld of oncology. For patients treated with lobectomy, ultrasound every 1 –3 years for 5 –8 years is appropriate if the initial study is negative; serial Tg monitoring is not recommended. If nodules remain in the residual lobe, follow-up per ATA nodule guidelines is advised. Recommendations for use of diagnostic whole-body RAI scan (WBS) have been revised (R49): diagnostic WBS is not recommended after thyroidectomy without RAI, or after hemithyroidectomy. In patients with intermediate-high and high-risk of recurrence, new guidelines recommend that WBS can be done if there is clinical suspicion for recurrence, rather than routinely 6 –12 months after RAI. SPECT-CT in addition to (rather than instead of) planar imaging is preferred for anatomical localization of RAI uptake.

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: Strong emphasis is placed on performing ongoing risk stratiﬁcation (response to therapy assessment) during long- term disease surveillance, which is an iterative process that informs surveillance intervals and therapeutic management decisions (R51 and Fig. 6 of the 2025 ATA Guidelines). Size is no longer considered the primary determinant for surgical treatment of recurrent/residual neck nodal disease, in favor of integration of multiple factors including location, pace of growth, and patient factors/preference. Percutaneous ethanol ablation and RFA are now explicitly mentioned as alternatives for managing recurrent/residual DTC in patients at high-risk for complications from reoperation (R52). RAI may be considered for isolated cervical lymph node metasta- ses after local therapy or if local therapy is contraindicated; EBRT may be considered for unresectable or extranodal/ soft-tissue invasive locoregional disease (R53). RAI remains an important treatment modality for recur- rent or residual locoregional/distant disease.

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: The 2025 guide- lines emphasize care with high ( >5.5 GBq/>150 mCi) doses of RAI in elderly patients and those with renal insuf ﬁciency, along with use of dosimetry to maximize ef ﬁcacy and safety if high doses are given (R55). RhTSH is now considered EXEC SUMMARY OF 2025 ATA GUIDELINES FOR DIFF THYCA 1219

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: equally acceptable to levothyroxine withdrawal for I-131 preparation for patients with distant metastases (R55). The designation of RAI-resistant (RAIR) DTC now requires prior treatment with at least one ablative dose of RAI (R59). Given controversies around the classi ﬁcation of RAIR-DTC and determination of what constitutes a clini- cally meaningful response, the 2025 guidelines are less deﬁnitive, highlighting that criteria suggesting refractory dis- ease should be used to gauge likelihood of responsiveness across a spectrum, rather than serving as de ﬁnitive evidence of treatment futility. RAIR DTC and use of systemic therapy For asymptomatic, stable, or minimally progressive RAIR metastatic DTC, disease monitoring with TSH-suppressive therapy remains an option (R60). Molecular testing is not rou- tinely recommended (R60) but should be performed in pro- gressive cases before systemic therapy (R61). Incorporation of molecular testing to determine initial management strategy for RAIR metastatic DTC reﬂects advances and FDA approvals of targeted therapies on actionable driver alterations such as NTRK, RET, ALK, and BRAF V600E (R62 –71).

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: The guide- lines also give a speciﬁc recommendation for ﬁrst line lenvati- nib at a starting dose of 24 mg per day, in most patients, and second line cabozantinib for RAIR DTC without actionable alterations (R62–66, R71). For patients with NTRK, RET, or ALK alterations, speciﬁc targeted therapy for each is recom- mended as ﬁrst line treatment, whereas BRAF V600E targeted therapy is recommended as second line, although it can be con- sidered ﬁrst line (R67–70). After progression on initial therapy, tissue sampling is recommended for molecular testing to clar- ify resistance (R72). For patients with high tumor mutational burden, mismatch repair-deﬁcient disease, or tumors with high microsatellite instability, immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy is recommended, reﬂecting tissue agnostic approval of ICI (R73). Redifferentiation therapy for MAPK pathway inhib- itor was added as a consideration (R74). Finally, cytotoxic chemotherapy remains an option for RAIR DTC in patients with rapidly progressive and symptomatic disease, though par- ticipation in a clinical trial is preferred in this setting (R75).

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: For solitary or oligometastatic (2–5 lesions) disease, focal abla- tive therapy can be considered (R76). For patients with site- speciﬁc symptoms, local therapy can be considered to alleviate symptoms (R77). Bone-modifying agents are still recom- mended for patients with multiple bone metastases (R78). For brain metastases, surgery and/or stereotactic body radiotherapy remain the mainstay of therapy (R79). Survivorship The 2025 guidelines newly recommend discussing potential long-term treatment effects—including voice changes, hypopar- athyroidism, scar appearance, neck tightness, dysphagia, psy- chosocial distress, fatigue,ﬁnancial impact, and cancer-related worry—with patients (R82). These issues should be incorpo- rated into shared decision-making and supported by access to high-quality resources such as s upport groups, guidance on managing distress, and local support services (R83–84). Conclusion The 2025 ATA guidelines represent a major evolution in the management of DTC, incorporating contemporary evi- dence, re ﬁned pathology classiﬁcation, and a more personal- ized, patient-centered approach.

chunks.title: ATA 2025 differentiated thyroid cancer executive summary
chunks.text: These updates are designed to support busy clinicians by providing concise, actionable recommendations that balance oncologic outcomes with qual- ity of life and long-term survivorship. Bible,1 Electron Kebebew,2 James Brierley,3 Juan P. Brito,4 Maria E. Cabanillas,5 Thomas J. Clark Jr.,6 Antonio Di Cristofano, 7 Robert Foote,8 Thomas Giordano,9 Jan Kasperbauer,10 Kate Newbold,11 Yuri E. Nikiforov,12 Gregory Randolph,13 M. Sara Rosenthal,14 Anna M. Sawka,15 Manisha Shah,16 Ashok Shaha,17 Robert Smallridge,18 and Carol K. Wong-Clark* Background: Anaplastic thyroid cancer (ATC) is a rare but highly lethal form of thyroid cancer. Since the guidelines for the management of ATC by the American Thyroid Association were ﬁrst published in 2012, signiﬁcant clinical and scientiﬁc advances have occurred in the ﬁeld. The aim of these guidelines is to inform clinicians, patients, and researchers on published evidence relating to the diagnosis and management of ATC. Methods: The speciﬁc clinical questions and topics addressed in these guidelines were based on prior versions of the guidelines, stakeholder input, and input of the Task Force members (authors of the guideline).

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Relevant literature was reviewed, including serial PubMed searches supplemented with additional articles. The American College of Physicians Guideline Grading System was used for critical appraisal of evidence and grading strength of recommendations. Results: The guidelines include the diagnosis, initial evaluation, establishment of treatment goals, approaches to locoregional disease (surgery, radiotherapy, targeted/systemic therapy, supportive care during active therapy), approaches to advanced/metastatic disease, palliative care options, surveillance and long-term monitoring, and ethical issues, including end of life. The guidelines include 31 recommendations and 16 good practice statements. Conclusions: We have developed evidence-based recommendations to inform clinical decision-making in the management of ATC. While all care must be individualized, such recommendations provide, in our opinion, optimal care paradigms for patients with ATC.

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: INTRODUCTION A merican Thyroid Association (ATA) guidelines for management of patients with anaplastic thyroid cancer (ATC) by Smallridge et al. (1) were published in 2012, being the ﬁrst major original work on this subject. In view of the advances in the ﬁeld of thyroid and other cancers and emerging concepts since that publication, we sought to craft comprehensive new guidelines for ATC based on sound methodology, evidence-based concepts, expert opinion, ethical principles, and sensitivity to the key im- portance of the wishes and concerns of patients, guided by their families and close loved ones, as they relate to the medical and professional care they receive. The ATA guidelines Task Force (the au thors of the guideline) for ATC was the impetus for the development of these guide- lines as they had a major inﬂuence on the authorship and provided administrative support. We were granted inde- pendence, however, in the creation of this work by the ATA. Moreover, as authors of an original work, we have assumed independence and accountability for its content.

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: The organization of these gu idelines is summarized in the Table of Contents, directing readers to content-speciﬁc text, recommendations, and go od practice statements de- veloped from the literature, reviewed and synthesized considering also expert opinion and input from patient advocates. Table 1 provides the key steps in the manage- ment of ATC, including guidance in attaining accurate di- agnosis, evaluation, and staging, followed promptly by establishing goals of care desired by the patient; ATC management strategies are thereafter indicated in Figure 1 (stage IVA and IVB) and in Figure 2 (stage IVC). These ﬂow diagrams are introduced early as a reference, with supporting evidence and nuanc es appearing in the pertinent corresponding text sections, and a summary of all the rec- ommendations, and good practice statements. Thyroid cancer incidence has increased in the United States (2). ATC is derived from follicular thyroid cells (‘‘thyrocytes’’) and is associated with the highest mortality risk of any thyroid-arising tumor, but accounts for only a small percentage of thyroid cancer cases overall (2).

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: In the United States, ATC is responsible for 1.7% of all thyroid cancers, while geographically, ATC accounts for 1.3% to 9.8% (median = 3.6%) of all thyroid cancers (3). In several countries, the incidence of ATC has decreased (4,5). The increasing diagnosis of papillary thyroid cancer (PTC) has increased the denominator of all detected thyroid cancers especially in developed countries, having the potential to decrease the percentage of all thyroid cancers accounted for by ATC. ATC patients have a historical median survival of about 5 months and a 1-year overall survival of 20% (3). All patients with ATC are classiﬁed by the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) TNM system as stage IV (A, B, or C) because of this universally poor historical prognosis; accordingly, counseling, deﬁning goals of care, and establishing a man- agement plan must be accomplished quickly. While all thy- roid cancer patients require a multidisciplinary team of specialists, the sudden onset and aggressive course of ATC necessitate the immediate and coordinated involvement of surgeons, radiation and medical oncologists/oncologic en- docrinologists, and palliative care teams.

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: METHODS General aims of the guidelines, target audiences, and stakeholder representation The overarching goal of these guidelines is to improve patient care with respect to the diagnosis and management of ATC predicated upon an ethical and patient-centered ap- proach, evidence-informed and encompassing structured literature reviews.

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: resulting draft document revised in accord with input from the ATA Board of Directors, Committees, and Membership. The target audiences of these guidelines are physicians caring for patients with ATC, health policy makers, and ATC patients and their families/partners. Contributors to these guidelines include physicians who specialize in oncologic endocrinology, endocrine surgery, head/neck surgery, nu- clear medicine, radiation oncology, medical oncology, pa- thology, the basic science of thyroid cancers, bioethics, guideline methodology, and patient advocate stakeholders. Table 1. Key Steps in the Management of Anaplastic Thyroid Cancer 1. Rapidly and deﬁnitively establish the diagnosis Because ATC is a highly dedifferentiated cancer that retains few characteristics of noncancerous thyroid cells, attaining a deﬁnitive diagnosis can be challenging, yet critical. Time is also of the essence because of the very rapid growth rate of ATC and due to the importance of early intervention in minimizing catastrophic airway compromise. /C15 Differential considerations/mimics can include primary thyroid lymphoma, SCC of the head and neck, and metastatic cancer (especially from lung).

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: /C15 Early assessment of tumor mutations is key in expanding therapeutic options. 2. Attain multidisciplinary team engagement and coordination Coordinate early multidisciplinary involvement of surgeons, radiation and medical oncologists, endocrinologists, and palliative care teams to arrive at options for best care as outlined below. 3. Determine extent of disease /C15 Staging with imaging is required to classify as stage IVA, IVB, IVC; this is best done with FDG PET/CT and/or alternatively with dedicated body CT or MRI. /C15 Extent of local invasion must also be evaluated in parallel to assist in surgical decision-making, and requires laryngoscopy. 4. Undertake patient counseling to establish individualized patient goals of care Counseling must be provided by a team/individuals skilled in the surgical, medical, and palliative management of complex thyroid malignancies in which trade-offs counterbalancing risks and beneﬁts with goals of care are completely discussed. This counseling should best involve not only the patient but also involve supportive individuals/family members. 5.

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Evaluate Surgical Options /C15 The primary goals in stages IVA and IVB ATC patients within an aggressive approach to their care are complete resection and prompt transition to adjuvant deﬁnitive-intention therapy, as long-term survival may be attainable. Thus, surgical procedures should not generate a wound or result in complications that would prevent chemotherapy and radiation onset due to the risk of wound breakdown given the lack of data supporting an association between increased extent of surgery and improved survival outcomes. /C15 In IVC ATC, the limited beneﬁt resulting from surgery must be carefully tempered in consideration of other available palliative approaches, including radiation and systemic therapy. 6. Surgical decision-making Rapidly assess resectability determining tumor invasion of the larynx, trachea, esophagus, and status of the major vessels of the neck. Consider the need for tracheotomy, extent of thyroidectomy, neck dissection, and the need to avoid laryngectomy, esophageal resection, and major vessel reconstruction.

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Balancing morbidity from surgery with expected beneﬁts within the context of patient-anticipated prognosis and individualized goals of care is paramount. Considerations: /C15 Performance score/status. /C15 Presence of distant metastasis. /C15 Extent of local invasion of trachea and esophagus. /C15 Need for urgent tracheostomy, understanding that placement of a tracheostomy results in immediate improvement in upper airway obstruction but requires signiﬁcant education for care and understanding that tumor location and growth may make management of the tracheotomy complex. /C15 Patient goals of care and willingness to accept anticipated morbidity of planned surgery. 7. Nonsurgical management decision-making Other than surgery, options may include postoperative or primary chemoradiation versus palliative radiotherapy, systemic therapy, or best supportive care considered within the context of: /C15 Patient goals of care and willingness to accept anticipated toxicities of presented options. /C15 Patient performance status and comorbidities and their impacts on feasibility of planned care. /C15 Trade-offs from one approach to care versus alternatives. 8.

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Keep hospice/end-of-life care discussions in the foreground /C15 Given the historically dire prognosis of ATC, especially if stage IVC, hospice should always be presented among care options. /C15 Truth telling and realistic presentation of anticipated prognosis are critical in allowing sound patient decisions within their individual goals of care. /C15 For some patients, hospice may be preferrable—even from the outset—in comparison with other alternative care options. ATC, anaplastic thyroid cancer; CT, computed tomography; FDG, ﬂuorodeoxyglucose; MRI, magnetic resonance imaging; PET, positron emission tomography; SCC, squamous cell carcinoma. chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: As a technical note, conﬂicts of authors’ institutions of employment were deemed nonexclusionary. No external funding from industry was received by the ATA or by authors for guideline development. Scope of the guideline and search for relevant litera- ture. In preparing these guidelines, we developed a con- sensus comprehensive list of questions covering the areas of ATC evaluation and diagnosis, ethics of ATC care, and es- tablishing patient goals of care, approaches to locoregional disease as well as to advanced/metastatic disease, palliative care/hospice, and surveillance and long-term monitoring. To maximize our deliberations, we developed consensus draft recommendations and solicited input from the ATA Board of Directors, ATA Guidelines and Statements Committee, and members of the ATA by posting them on the members-only section of the ATA website www.thyroid.org. Input of all authors, including expert clinicians and patient advocates, ATC researchers, and methodologists—as well as from the ATA Board of Directors and ATA members—was vetted and discussed and a set of questions were drafted by the cochairs (E.K. and K.C.B.).

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: The list of questions was circulated elec- tronically to all authors, revised as needed, and all authors agreed on the list of seminal questions. For any questions for which systematic reviews were planned, methodologists (J.P.B. and A.M.S.) provided input on structuring of questions using the PICO format (‘‘patient, intervention, comparator, outcome’’), or other formats as applicable. To identify relevant literature that might assist in preparing this document as comprehensively as possible, a medical reference librarian consulted with a panel members and de- signed and executed a search of several databases, including the following: Ovid Medline In-Process and Other Non- Indexed Citations, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, Ovid Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Ovid Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, and Scopus. Databases were searched from inception to the date of the search (February 15, 2017, initially and updated in May 11, 2020), without restriction of publication date or language (search strategy in Supplementary Data S2).

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: The search was supplemented by handsearching the resulting reference lists from eligible included studies, and based upon additional references forwarded by Task Force members. A total of 3064 articles were identiﬁed, of which 205 studies were deemed as the most relevant literature, but none of these articles included a randomized clinical trial. Expert panelists also provided additional studies for consideration, from re- spective personal records and from publications emerging during guideline development. Review and grading of the evidence. Systematic re- views on the topics of surgery, external beam radiation therapy, and systemic therapies for management of ATC were commissioned by the ATA from the Mayo Evidence- Based Practice group ( J.P.B.). In addition, expert panelists reviewed relevant literature from the search and from per- sonal records. The authors of respective sections drafted recommendations and explained the rationale for the rec- ommendations in accompanying supporting text, enhanced by input from the entire panel.

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: The quality and strength of the authors’ recommendations based on the body of evidence were reported using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) Group, GRADE workgroup sys- tem; a detailed description of the grading scheme has been published elsewhere (6). In this system, recommendations are classiﬁed as strong or conditional. Strong recommendations (‘‘we recommend’’) are those in which the panel is conﬁdent that the anticipated desirable effects of following a recom- mendation clearly outweigh undesirable effects and that the recommendation should be implemented into practice. Conditional recommendations (‘‘we suggest’’) are those in which the panel concludes that the anticipated desirable ef- fects of following these recommendations probably outweigh undesirable effects, but is not conﬁdent about this conclusion and there may be reasonable alternative options for consid- eration in clinical practice. Importantly, however, these are guidelines, indicating that nuances of individual patients must shape implementation. One factor that inﬂuences the strength of recommendations is the quality of the body of supportive evidence.

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: In the GRADE system, there are four categories of quality of evi- dence: high quality, moderate quality, low quality, and very low quality (6,7). High-quality evidence on therapeutic in- terventions requires one or more studies at low risk of bias (e.g., randomized-controlled trials [RCTs] without important limitations), that have consistent results and precise estima- tes. Very low-quality evidence derives from studies at high risk of bias (e.g., observational), or inconsistent and impre- cise results across studies. Along with the quality of the body of evidence, the authors considered a balance between ben- eﬁts, risks, and burdens of interventions as an important factor in deciding the strength of the recommendation. The strength of the recommendation is correlated with the quality of evidence. For instance, strong recommendations are usually supported by moderate- or high-quality evidence. Nevertheless, we were frequently able to make strong rec- ommendations based on low-quality evidence. The GRADE system offers ﬁve distinct situations where these types of recommendations are appropriate.

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: The adherence to these paradigmatic situations by these guidelines is shown in Supplementary Data S3. When the authors deemed that there was a large body of indi rect evidence to support the beneﬁt of a recommendation, and in which the evaluation of ANAPLASTIC THYROID CANCER GUIDELINES 341 Downloaded by 2001:4450:819a:3900:88e4:1a52:aa93:d0c5 from www.liebertpub.com at 11/05/24. chunks.text: alternatives in clinical trials would be unproductive and unnecessary, the authors provided good practice statements (7,8). These good practice recommendations are developed based on the authors’ expert opinion, without a formal lit- erature search, that there is sufﬁcient indirect evidence to provide high certainty that the recommendation will result in more desirable than undesirable effects. As such, good practice recommendations are actionable statements that the authors feel are necessary, but are not appropriate for rating the quality of evidence. Good practice recommendations are different than strong recommendations with low-quality evidence, as the latter are recommendations that panelists judge to be applicable to the majority of patients despite warranting low or very low certainty.

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: To identify good practice statements, the authors applied the following cri- teria: (i) the message was necessary, (ii) after consideration of all relevant outcomes and potential downstream conse- quences, implementing the g ood practice statement will result in large net positive consequences, (iii) collecting and summarizing the evidence was poor use of a guideline panel’s limited time and energy, and (iv) there was a well- documented, clear, and explic it rationale connecting the indirect evidence (9). An experienced GRADE methodol- ogist ( J.P.B.) oversaw the grading of all recommendations and the quality of evidence. Consensus procedure. Recommendations, good prac- tice statements, and supporting text were electronically dis- tributed to all authors, and thereafter discussed as a group on monthly or bimonthly conference calls as well as during several in-person meetings. During or shortly after confer- ence calls/meetings, a revised document was circulated to all authors for additional input, comment, and suggestions for further revisions.

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Any additional necessary revisions were incorporated and discussed, and, if no further changes were requested, a consensus of the group was assumed. Many sections of this document were reviewed iteratively during calls two to three times, and any author could at any point ask to revisit any section. Upon completion of all sections of the guidelines, a list of all of the recommendations and good practice statements, as well as the entire guideline document, was circulated to all authors, with further opportunity for revision or rewording, as needed. Once no further revisions were requested or deemed necessary by the guideline co- chairs, consensus on the entire document was achieved. The experienced GRADE methodologist ( J.P.B.) checked all recommendations and good practice statements to ensure they were consistent with the GRADE approach.

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Uniform (100%) consensus was obtained among the group on the wording and strength of all recommendations, however, gi- ven the technicalities involved in critically appraising evi- dence and operationalizing the GRADE system, the ﬁnal decisions on the quality of evidence or the appropriate ap- plication of the good practice statement category were de- ferred to the GRADE methodologist ( J.P.B.). Patient representative advisor involvement in the guideline development process. Patient representative advisors (T.J.C. and C.K.W.-C.) were fully involved in the guideline development process, including contributing input on questions, text, and recommend ations and formally voting on recommendations. However, patient representative ad- visors were able to defer to other expert authors on speciﬁc technical scientiﬁc aspects of any recommendation that was beyond their comfort level. An important role of patient representative advisors was providing input on Values Statements.

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: In the process of discussing recommendations, if the patient representative advisors believed there were important considerations re garding values that should be communicated (beyond that described in the recommenda- tion and the text describing the evidence basis for the rec- ommendation), Values Statements were proposed. Values Statements were intended to complement the presentation of accompanying recommendations and descriptions of the evidence and were not graded themselves. All panel mem- bers had the opportunity to contribute to the wording of Values Statements, and consensus was reached among the group (in a similar process to that of recommendations) on the ﬁnal Values Statements. Staging system used in the guidelines. The AJCC Can- cer Staging Manual (8th Edition) Residual Tumor (R) Clas- siﬁcation was used to assess surgical effects on outcomes across the studies reviewed. Terms and deﬁnitions TNM staging. All ATCs are stage 4 (AJCC 8th Edition). Stage IVA lesions (T1-T3a, N0, M0) are still localized within the thyroid gland and have not deﬁnitely spread to lymph nodes (N0) or to distant sites (M0).

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: In Stage IVB ATC, the primary tumor has grown outside/through the thyroid capsule (T3b, T4) and/or is involving locoregional lymph nodes (‡N1), but it has not spread to distant sites (M0). In Stage IVC (Any T, Any N, M1) , the tumor has spread to distant site(s). Extent of resection. R0 designates complete resection with negative microscopic margins, R1 designates complete resection of all grossly visible tumors but with involved surgical resection margins (m icroscopically involved re- section margins), and R2 designates resection in which gross cancer was left in place (macroscopically involved resection margins). Adjuvant therapy and neoadjuvant therapy. Radiation, systemic therapy, or the combination givenafter surgery with curative intention is referred to as adjuvant therapy ; and when given before surgery, neoadjuvant therapy. Oligometastatic disease. Some cancers are associated with only a small number of macrometastases (termed oli- gometastatic cancer). In genera l, most studies of oligome- tastatic cancer have included patients with one to ﬁve distinct metastases.

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: With a limited number of metastases, it becomes theoretically possible to treat detectable tumors with curative intention using surgery and/or locally ablative therapies, realizing that occult metastatic disease may nevertheless exist. Deﬁnition of therapeutic terms Standard radiation prescription. The unit dose of radia- tion is the Gray, abbreviated to Gy. Some prescriptions are given in centiGray or cGy (1 Gy = 100 cGy). A radiation prescription describes the total dose of radiation to be 342 BIBLE ET AL. Downloaded by 2001:4450:819a:3900:88e4:1a52:aa93:d0c5 from www.liebertpub.com at 11/05/24. chunks.text: delivered, the number of fractions (number of daily treat- ments), the dose of each daily treatment, and the overall length of the treatment course. The usual daily fraction size is 1.8 or 2 Gy. A standard prescription in the setting of neck irradiation in ATC would be, for instance: 66 Gy over 61/2 weeks, given as 33 daily fractions of 2 Gy per day, 5 days a week for deﬁnitive treatment, but this is adjusted depending on the clinical setting as discussed later in the document. Altered fractionation. Altered fractionation implies a lar- ger number of fractions ( hyperfractionated), or a smaller number of fractions ( hypofractionated), or a shorter overall treatment time ( accelerated). By using hyperfractionated treatment with more than one daily fraction given, it enables the prescription to be given over a shorter treatment time (accelerated hyperfractionated radiotherapy ). In a rapidly growing tumor such as ATC, accelerating the treatment has the potential to minimize tumor growth that may occur over the radiotherapy treatment course. By giving multiple small fractions, the toxicity may also be reduced.

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: An example of an accelerated hyperfractionated prescription would be: 60 Gy over 4 weeks given as 40 twice-daily fractions of 1.5 Gy, 5 days a week. Radiotherapy dose. There are many different potential radiation prescription doses; for the purpose of this report they have been grouped as deﬁnitive-intention or palliative- intention. Deﬁnitive-intention radiotherapy is high-dose radiation given with or without concurrent chemotherapy with the in- tent of maximizing the chance of long-term local control. Examples range from 50 Gy in 20 fractions, 2.5 Gy per fraction over 4 weeks at the low end, to 70 Gy in 35 fractions, 2 Gy per fraction over 7 weeks at the high end. Palliative- intention Radiotherapy is lower dose radiotherapy given over a shorter time period with the primary aim of improving local symptoms and achieving initial disease control while mini- mizing hospital/clinic visits. This may be directed to the primary tumor or to metastases. Typical examples could be 20 Gy in 5 fractions, 4 Gy per fraction over 1 week and 30 Gy in 10 fractions, 3 Gy per fraction over 2 weeks. Conformal radiation.

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: In conformal radiotherapy, the vol- ume treated is tailored to and ‘‘conforms’’ to the shape of the tumor. The toxicity of radiation to the surrounding normal tissues is thereby reduced. Intensity-modulated radiotherapy. By modulating the in- tensity of the radiation ﬁelds as well as shape of the ﬁelds, the radiation can be made more conformal (tailored), thereby reducing toxicity to the adjacent normal structures and po- tentially enabling a higher radiation dose to be given to the tumor areas. Radiosurgery and stereotactic body radiotherapy (ste- reotactic radiosurgeries). Radiosurgery and stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) are highly conformal/focused radiation that allows a single large fraction of radiation to be given. Stereotactic radiosurgery usually refers to radio- surgery to the brain (e.g., Gamma Knife/C210). Stereotactic body radiosurgery usually refers to radiosurgery to parts of the body other than to the brain (e.g., CyberKnife /C210, X-Knife/C210) and SBRT usually refers to highly conformal radiotherapy given in 3 to 10 fractions. Concurrent chemoradiation.

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Some chemotherapeutic agents when given concurrently with radiation can potentiate the antitumor effects of radiation and thereby act as ‘‘radia- tion sensitizers.’’ This therapeutic advantage may be at the cost of increased toxicity, and in some regimens may require a reduction of the radiation dose. The principal aim of che- motherapy given concurrently with radiation is to increase the chance of local control of the tumor, and also with the intentions to affect more rapid tumor cytoreduction (assum- ing that the systemic therapy involved may be active in ATC) and, aspirationally, in parallel to control systemic micro- metastatic disease if present. Chemotherapy. Chemotherapy, for the purposes of these guidelines, denotes cytotoxic agents that target basic cellular components and processes that are commonly altered in cancers. Examples include agents targeted toward cell divi- sion machinery (e.g., antimicrotubule inhibitors, paclitaxel and docetaxel), DNA repair pathways (e.g., topoisomerase inhibitors and poly-adenosine diphosphate ribose polymerase inhibitors), or DNA structure (e.g., platins). Genomic tumor assessment.

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Genomic tumor assessment denotes rigorous analysis of tumor DNA for the purposes of deﬁning altered genes of potential or actual relevance to cancer growth and/or survival. Various platforms are avail- able for this assessment, each with their own strengths and weakness as discussed in the Diagnosis of ATC section. Genetically informed targeted therapy. ‘‘Targeted thera- py’’ denotes systemic treatment intended to be speciﬁcally directed toward an actually or presumed altered molecule or pathway relevant to cancer growth or survival. In general, an agent or agents are selected to target a speciﬁcally identiﬁed ‘‘driver’’ mutation. Bridging therapy. ‘‘Bridging therapy’’ is used to denote interim approaches to the treatment of general applicability in ATC intended to contain disease while information is being attained that may better inform subsequent individualization of systemic therapy such as via targeted approaches. Response evaluation criteria in solid tumor response. Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) are used to assess objectively the effects of systemic therapy on tumor dimensions/size (10).

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: After determining the baseline diameters of index lesions (must be >1 cm for visceral le- sions, >1.5 cm short axis for nodal metastases; only two measured lesions per disease site/organ allowed, generally the largest) with cross-sectional imaging (computed tomog- raphy [CT], magnetic resonance imaging [MRI]), follow-up measurements of the same lesions are determined at deﬁned intervals and compared with baseline as a percentage of the sum of all index lesions. A complete response (CR) means disappearance of all lesions; a partial response (PR) is at least a 30% reduction in the lesional sum, conﬁrmed at least once at a ‡4-week interval once observed; progressive disease (PD) is a 20% or greater increase in lesional sum from baseline or nadir; and stable disease (SD) refers to tumors not reaching criteria for either PR or PD. Of note is that these criteria require the absence of new locations of disease and the absence of growth of any nontarget lesions. chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: DISCLAIMERS AND GENERAL GUIDANCE In line with, and echoing the ofﬁcial policies of the ATA, our recommendations and good practice statements cannot be ‘‘all things to all people’’ from the methodological stand- point. It is not possible to use and reconcile all proper methodological approaches due to inherent and irreconcil- able differences in various utilized and acceptable competing guideline methodologies. These guidelines do not establish a standard of care, replace sound clinical judgment, or capture all nuances likely to be present in any particular patient, and speciﬁc outcomes are not guaranteed. We recommend that treatment decisions be based on independent judgments of health care providers carefully considering each patient’s individual circumstances and the goals of care (established at the outset and revisited frequently), as well as feasibility considerations (including regional access to speciﬁc health care resources). Our guideline recommendations are not in- tended to take the place of best physician judgment in diag- nosing and treating particular patients, or to supplant patient directives.

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: We expect that those who use these guidelines will consider them as an aid in, not a replacement for, sound and thoughtful clinical decision-making, with full consideration of each patient’s individuality in terms of history and phys- ical traits, comorbidities, functional status, and goals of care. REVIEW AND RECOMMENDATIONS ATC risk factors ATC is an aggressive tumor with a poor prognosis (3,11–14); median survival is 5–6 months and the 1-year survival is *20% (3,13). Patients with ATC rarely survive more than 2 years after diagnosis. Reports suggest that between 3% and 10% survive more than 10 years. For example, Lam et al. re- ported a 10-year survival rate of ATC in China of*3% (15), while another case series reported that*10% of patients with ATC remained free of disease at 10, 12, and 13 years after treatment (16). Given its poor prognosis, identifying any po- tential risk factors for ATC has the potential to inform strategies to prevent this malignancy or allow early detection. Case/control studies are the most effective approach used to identify risk factors for different conditions, but are scarce in ATC.

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: In one case/control study of 126 patients with ATC and 252 controls individually matched by sex, age, and place of residence found in multivariate logistic regression anal- ysis that low education level (odds ratio [OR] 1.42, 95% conﬁdence interval [CI 1.09–1.86]), type B blood group (OR 2.41, [CI 1.03–5.66]), or goiter (OR 25–33, [CI 5.66– 126.65]) was associated with higher ATC risk (17). In a similar study, but using in the control group patients oper- ated for goiter, they noticed that a lower level of education (OR 1.85, [CI 1.21–2.82]) and type B blood group (OR 3.69, [CI 1.10–12.49]) continued to be risk factors for ATC (18). Association between education and ATC might be explained by confounding variables such as access to care and lower health awareness triggering neglected thyroid conditions with potential to link to increased chances of ATC pathogenesis; however, the biological explanation for the association between ATC and blood type remains unclear. The reason for the observed association of goiter with ATC is uncertain, but could reﬂect at least two possible contribu- tory factors.

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: First, there are some data that iodine deﬁciency, a known predisposing condition for goiter, may also be a risk factor for ATC—based, in part, upon data indicating de- creasing ATC incidence associated with public health effort to introduce food iodination in European and South America nations (19,20). Such data are, however, confounded of course by many factors also drifting over the time of such public health efforts. Second, one might alternatively spec- ulate that neglected goiters among medically underserved communities might have the potential to lead to higher ATC risk, potentially thereby also linking lower socioeconomic status and goiter to each other and to ATC. Two systematic reviews and meta-analyses (21,22) and one pooled analysis of prospective studies (23) have reported a positive association between measures of adiposity and risk of thyroid cancer, including small subgroup analyses in ATC. Schmidet al.reported, based on data from three studies, that the relative risk of ATC (with CI) was 1.93 [CI 1.23–3.02] relative to lean patients according to the World Health Organization (WHO) obesity body mass index (BMI) classiﬁcation (21). Ma et al.

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: similarly reported that, based on data from three studies, the relative risk of ATC in obese patients was 1.93 ([CI 1.23– 3.03], p = 0.004) relative to lean patients (22). Kitahara et al. reported that the hazard ratio (HR) for ATC in obesity was 1.43 [CI 1.09–1.89], restricted to BMI values between 15.0 and 59.9 kg/m2, including data from 19 ATC cases (23). More and larger studies are needed to conﬁrm these ﬁndings, incorpo- rating adjustments for relevant confounders. A very small subset of differentiated thyroid cancer (DTC) transforms to ATC, supporting the view that DTC is a risk factor for ATC. Oishi et al. recently retrospectively compared the clinicopathological and molecular features in histopathology specimens from 27 ATC cases that contained antecedent PTC with that of 92 archived PTC cases (without ATC) (24). The rarity of anaplastic transformation of PTC is reﬂected by the fact that these authors had to screen 11,480 cases of PTC and 228 cases of ATC, to identify 27 cases of anaplastic transformation of PTC.

chunks.title: ATA 2021 anaplastic thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: In a multivariable analy- sis, the TERT promoter mutation (C228T) was the only factor independently implicated as potentially associated with anaplastic transformation of PTC (OR 68.18, [CI 13.97–332], p < 0.001, adjusted for age, sex, and BRAFV600E mutation) (24). Furthermore, Oishi et al. validated their ﬁndings using publicly available data from the Cancer Genome Atlas study, and in this data set found that in mul- tivariate analysis, age >60 years (OR 4.87; [CI 1.17–20.37]) and TERT promoter mutation (OR 39.48; [CI 7.93–196.56]) were independently associated with anaplastic transforma- tion of PTC (but not BRAFV600E, p = 0.066) (24). Genomic studies of poorly differentiated thyroid cancer (PDTC) and ATC provide evidence for a model of tumorigenesis in which ATCs arise from preexisting DTC, via the accumu- lation of additional somatic genetic alterations (25), in- cluding TP53 and TERT promoter mutations. DIAGNOSIS OF ATC: CYTOLOGY AND CORE BIOPSY, HISTOPATHOLOGY, AND DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS Cytology and pathology procedures Fine needle aspiration and core biopsy. Fine needle as- piration (FNA) is generally the ﬁrst type of biopsy attempted 344 BIBLE ET AL.
