chunks.text: current recommendation that ﬁrst-line pembrolizumab is not recommended). Clinical interpretation. Combining lenvatinib with pembrolizumab may enhance immune activation and anti- tumor effects, whereby MKIs may modulate the tumor microenvironment to improve response to immune check- point blockade. However, durable tumor regression in low- mutation-burden tumors such as differentiated thyroid cancers is not established. Second-line therapies for such patients are relatively limited and are toxic, especially when initiating treatment at the approved starting dosage of an MKI. Thus, pembrolizumab may be added to treatment in patients who have disease progression on a dosage of len- vatinib that was previously sustaining a disease response and whose MKI-related side effects were well managed. Question 4 In patients with RAI-refractory, well-differentiated thyroid cancer (papillary, follicular, oncocytic), cytotoxic chemo- therapy compared to targeted agents or MKIs impact re- sponse and/or survival in the ﬁrst-line and subsequent-line setting? Recommendation 4.1 Literature review and analysis.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Doxorubicin, either as a single agent or in combination with cisplatin, has been associated with only modest responses in the treatment of RAI-refractory, differentiated thyroid cancers. Speciﬁcally, one randomized trial of doxorubicin (n 5 41) versus com- bination doxorubicin and cisplatin (n 5 43) demonstrated a 17% (n 5 7) response rate for monotherapy and 26% (n 5 6) for the combination. 80 Clinical interpretation. Cytotoxic chemotherapy has a limited role in the management of RAI-refractory, well- differentiated thyroid cancer. Doxorubicin, the only US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)–approved cytotoxic therapy, should only be considered in patients with meta- static, rapidly progressive, symptomatic, or imminently threatening disease that is not amenable to control by other treatment modalities, including surgery, radiation, MKIs, or genomically targeted therapy. The use of cytotoxic therapy as frontline therapy is not recommended outside the context of clinical trials. Recommendation 4.2 Literature review and analysis. There is scarcity of data in support of cytotoxic chemotherapy in this population.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: There are randomized data that demonstrated modest re- sponse rates (approximately 20%-25%) as cited previously, but there is limited evidence regarding the use of these medications in the context of targeted therapies. Clinical interpretation. Cytotoxic chemotherapy should only be for patients with metastatic, rapidly progressive, symptomatic, or imminently threatening disease not oth- erwise amenable to control through other approaches, in- cluding kinase inhibitors, preferably within the context of a therapeutic clinical trial. Doxorubicin is the only cytotoxic approved agent for thyroid cancer. Its activity in the treatment of RAI-refractory, differentiated thyroid cancer, however, is very modest with infrequent, short-lived re- sponses. Furthermore, combination regimens with doxo- rubicin and cisplatin have been explored without clear bene ﬁt over single-agent doxorubicin with increased toxicity. DIFFERENTIATED HIGH-GRADE OR POORLY DIFFERENTIATED Prior to 2022, the term PDTC was used to describe follicular cell neoplasms exhibiting limited follicular differentiation and intermediate behavior between differentiated and un- differentiated (anaplastic) thyroid carcinoma.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Various di- agnostic criteria, such as the Turin proposal and Hiltzik’s histologic grade, deﬁned PDTC based on pathological fea- tures including absence of papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC)–like nuclei, mitotic index, growth pattern, and tumor necrosis. The WHO ﬁfth edition Classiﬁcation of Endocrine and Neuroendocrine Tumors introduced a new diagnostic cate- gory called DHGTC. 81 This category includes papillary, fol- licular, and oncocytic thyroid carcinomas with high-grade features (tumor necrosis, mitotic index) and a prognosis similar to that of PDTC. Consequently, the broader group termed high-grade follicular cell–derived nonanaplastic thyroid carcinoma now encompasses both PDTC (commonly RAS mutation–positive and lacks conventional PTC nuclear features) and DHGTC (PTCs in this group are commonly BRAF V600E mutation–positive and show diagnostic nuclear features). The following recommendations are largely derived from small subgroups of PDTC or DHGTC that were included in larger studies of well-differentiated and ATC. To be in- cluded in evidence tables for the PDTC or DHGTC sections, studies were required to explicitly state the inclusion of at least 10 patients with PDTC.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Although these studies gen- erally did not report outcomes speciﬁcally for the PDTC subgroup, overall conclusions from the study (eg, beneﬁt o f MKI over placebo) were thought to be generalizable to PDTC. There is lack of standardization and signiﬁcant heteroge- neity in the deﬁnitions of PDTC included in these trials, most of which were conducted prior to the WHO ﬁfth edition classiﬁcation. chunks.text: what should be recommended in the ﬁrst-line and subsequent-line setting? Recommendation 5.1 Literature review and analysis. Three RCTs that com- pared MKI to placebo in the ﬁrst-line RAI-refractory setting for DTC, which also included ≥10 patients with explicitly labeled PDTC, were reviewed. 44-46 In the phase III SELECT trial, lenvatinib led to a PFS beneﬁt (18.3 v 3.6 months; HR, 0.21) compared to placebo in the overall population; out- comes for the PDTC subgroup (28 patients in the lenvatinib arm, and 19 in the placebo arm) were not reported sepa- rately. 45 In the phase III DECISION trial, sorafenib also led to a PFS beneﬁt (modiﬁed PFS [mPFS] 10.8 v 5.8 months; HR, 0.59) compared to placebo in the overall population; again, results in the PDTC subgroup (24 patients in the sorafenib arm, 16 in placebo) were not reported separately. 44 Finally, in a randomized phase II trial comparing vandetanib to pla- cebo, the overall population had a PFS beneﬁt (HR, 0.63; mPFS 11.1 v 5.9 months); the subgroup including follicular (n 5 20) and PDTC (n 5 57) had a PFS HR of 0.83 favoring vandetanib.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: 46 Notably, a subsequent randomized phase III trial comparing vandetanib to placebo did not show a sig- niﬁcant PFS beneﬁt 82 ; this study was not formally included because the number of patients with PDTC was not explicitly stated. Several other studies including retrospective studies and prospective clinical trials for both DTC and ATC were reviewed, but either did not report the number of patients with PDTC or included fewer than 10 patients with PDTC. 5,37,79,83,84 In particular, the ATLEP study of lenvatinib and pembrolizumab included 27 patients with ATC and eight patients with PDTC, in whom 6/8 (75%) achieved partial response and 2/8 (25%) achieved stable disease 85 ; however, the full results of this study have not been pub- lished to date. A more recent study of lenvatinib with pembrolizumab also showed promising outcomes (mPFS 26.8 months in MKI-na ¨ ıve patients and 10.0 months in patients who have disease progression on lenvatinib), but also included only eight patients with PDTC and did not meet criteria for inclusion. 79 Clinical interpretation.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: The results of the prospective randomized trials conﬁrm that MKI leads to improved PFS compared to placebo for ﬁrst-line RAI-refractory DTC, and likely also provide beneﬁt in patients with PDTC or DHGTC. In particular, lenvatinib has a moderate quality of evidence supporting its use, given more impressive PFS beneﬁt compared to sorafenib or vandetanib. Thus, for patients with driver mutation–negative PDTC or DHGTC with RAI-refractory and progressive disease re- quiring systemic therapy, lenvatinib or sorafenib may be considered. Lenvatinib with pembrolizumab may be con- sidered for patients with aggressive PDTC or DHGTC, but there is insufﬁcient evidence to formally recommend this strategy. Recommendation 5.2 Literature review and analysis. The literature review did not yield any prospective or retrospective studies of MKI in the subsequent-line setting speciﬁcally for PDTC or DHGTC. COSMIC-311, 73 which established cabozantinib as second- line therapy, RAI-refractory, differentiated thyroid cancer, included fewer than 10 patients with PDTC and thus did not meet criteria for inclusion as part of the evidence base for this guideline. Clinical interpretation.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: The COSMIC-311 trial demon- strated that cabozantinib signiﬁcantly improved PFS in patients with previously treated RAI-refractory, differenti- ated thyroid cancer. However, due to the lack of dedicated trials in the PDTC population, there is currently insufﬁcient evidence to formally recommend cabozantinib as a standard second-line treatment. Question 6 In patients with RAI-refractory DHGTC or PDTC, do genomically targeted therapies compared to placebo or ob- servation impact survival in the ﬁrst-line and subsequent- line setting? Recommendation 6.1 Literature review and analysis. The literature review did not yield any prospective or retrospective studies of genomically targeted therapies in the ﬁrst-line or subsequent-line setting speciﬁcally for PDTC or DHGTC. While PDTC has a lower rate of actionable genomic alter- ations, DHGTCs may harbor BRAF V600E, NTRK, o r RET alterations. None of the prospective clinical trials of targeted therapies (dabrafenib or trametinib for BRAF V600E, sel- percatinib for RET, larotrectinib or entrectinib for NTRK) included 10 or more patients with explicitly labeled PDTC.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Please refer to the differentiated thyroid cancer section for guidelines on targeted therapies for driver mutation–posi- tive differentiated thyroid cancer. Clinical interpretation. For patients with DHGTC or PDTC that harbor an actionable genomic alteration, targeted therapies extrapolated from the differentiated thyroid cancer section may be considered; however, there is insuf- ﬁcient evidence to formally recommend this. chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Recommendation 7.1 Literature review and analysis. The literature review did not yield any prospective or retrospective studies of im- munotherapy in the ﬁrst-line or subsequent-line setting speciﬁcally for PDTC or DHGTC. A prospective study of ipilimumab and nivolumab for aggressive thyroid carci- noma 5 as well as the previously mentioned studies of len- vatinib and pembrolizumab 79,85 all included <10 patients with PDTC and did not report analysis within this patient subgroup. Clinical interpretation. The combination of lenvatinib with pembrolizumab and the use of ipilimumab or nivolu- mab are emerging therapeutic strategies that may be con- sidered for patients with PDTC. This is primarily based on extrapolation of data from studies conducted in the broader, patient population with RAI-refractory, differentiated thy- roid cancer. The underlying biological hypothesis is that PDTC or DHGTC, which shares characteristics of aggressive differentiated thyroid cancer, might beneﬁt similarly from these systemic approaches.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: However, while these combi- nations represent plausible therapeutic avenues, the current evidence base only supports their conditional consideration as treatment options, and there is insufﬁcient evidence to issue a formal recommendation for their routine use in clinical practice. Question 8 In patients with RAI-refractory DHGTC or PDTC, does cy- totoxic chemotherapy compared to targeted agents or MKIs impact response and/or survival and what should be rec- ommended in the ﬁrst-line and subsequent-line setting? Recommendation 8.1 Literature review and analysis. The literature review did not yield any prospective or retrospective studies of cyto- toxic chemotherapy in the ﬁrst-line or subsequent-line setting speciﬁcally for PDTC or DHGTC. Historical studies of cytotoxic chemotherapy either did not specify the number of or had fewer than 10 patients with PDTC. A more recent study of salvage pemetrexed-carboplatin in patients with refractory advanced thyroid cancer included seven patients with differentiated thyroid cancer or PDTC. 49 Clinical interpretation.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: There is insufﬁcient evidence to recommend cytotoxic chemotherapy for PDTC or DHGTC; however, regimens such as carboplatin or pemetrexed, taxanes, or doxorubicin may be considered in cases after disease progression on alternate systemic therapies. ANAPLASTIC (ATC) ATC requires a multidiscip linary approach to therapy in- cluding surgery, radiation, systemic therapy, and airway management. The workup should be swift and include stabilization of the airway, determination of the BRAF V600E status, stage, and resectability. In general, patients with stage IVA and IVB cancers without a BRAF V600E mutation should undergo surgery when feasible and then complete radiation to the neck with radiosensitizing che- motherapy. Patients with stage IVB with BRAF V600E mutation should be offered upfront neoadjuvant therapy, followed by surgery when possible, and radiation with radiosensitizing chemotherapy. Patients with stage IVC BRAF V600E mutations should be considered for BRAF- directed systemic therapy. These cases are more complex, and their treatment requires consideration of palliative radiation to the neck versus upfront systemic therapy when the airway is stable.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: The following recommendations pertain to the use of sys- temic therapy within this context. Question 9 In patients with ATC, do MKIs compared to placebo or ob- servation impact survival and what is recommended in the ﬁrst-line setting and subsequent-line setting? Recommendation 9.1 Literature review and analysis. Three prospective studies have evaluated the efﬁcacy of single-agent lenvatinib. 62,63,66 The largest study reported a 1-year sur- vival rate of 11.9% among 42 patients with ATC. 63 Further- more, prospective evaluations of patients with ATC without a genomic mutation treated with checkpoint inhibition demonstrate similarly poor median OS of 6.2 months. 66 A prospective, single-arm, phase II clinical trial investigated the combination of lenvatinib and pembrolizumab in 25 patients with ATC 61 without a BRAF V600 mutation; 96% of patients received either surgery or radiation to the primary tumor prior to study entry. The primary end point was median OS by at least 3 months compared to the historical benchmark of 3-month median OS observed with single- agent lenvatinib from a prior phase II clinical trial.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: 62 The study met its primary end point with median OS in the combination trial of 11.4 months (95% CI, 7.8 to 35.6; P < .025). The best overall response in target lesions was 36%. Serious adverse events, speciﬁcally bleeding and ﬁstula formation, were rare but occurred, warranting caution when considering this regimen in patients at risk for these complications. Clinical interpretation. Despite being based on a single- arm, nonrandomized study, the magnitude of survival beneﬁt compared to historical outcomes supports the use of lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab as a preferred systemic option for patients with metastatic, nongenomically altered ATC. Given the high mortality rate of ATC, the improved survival and acceptable response rate (36%) justify this approach, while acknowledging the need for careful toxicity monitoring, particularly concerning bleeding and ﬁstula formation. chunks.text: Recommendation 9.2 Literature review and analysis. There is no published literature identiﬁed evaluating second-line therapy after disease progression on lenvatinib or lenvatinib plus pem- brolizumab for ATC without a genomic mutation. Clinical interpretation. The absence of dedicated litera- ture regarding second-line treatment options after disease progression on lenvatinib or lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab for ATC without a genomic mutation creates a signiﬁcant therapeutic challenge. Disease usually progresses quickly after ﬁrst-line therapy; clinicians must carefully weigh the marginal beneﬁt of further systemic therapy against the potential for treatment-related toxicity and make best supportive care a critical component of the discussion. Palliation of symptoms of uncontrolled cancer should be prioritized. Patients are recommended to participate in a clinical trial. Question 10 In patients with ATC, do genomically targeted therapies compared to placebo or observation impact survival and what should be recommended in the ﬁrst-line and subsequent-line setting? Recommendation 10.1 Literature review and analysis.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Seven studies with BRAF V600E–directed targeted therapy alone or in combination with anti–PD-1 or PD-L1 immunotherapy were included. No randomized trials were found. All trials were single-arm prospective 52-54 or retrospective series. 56-59 The largest of the prospective trials with targeted therapy alone (dabra- fenib and trametinib) included 36 patients, while the largest retrospective series with combination BRAF V600E–tar- geted therapy plus immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy versus BRAF V600E–targeted therapy alone included 71 patients. 54 Median PFS and OS were 6.7 and 14.5 months, respectively, and the response rate was 58% in patients with conﬁrmed BRAF V600E mutation. In the retrospective trial, there were 23 patients treated with BRAF V600E–directed therapy alone, and the median OS was 9 months. The pa- tients in this study never received immune checkpoint in- hibitor therapy nor surgical resection after starting dabrafenib and trametinib. Similarly, the other retrospective trials showed a median OS of 6.9 to 10.7 months.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: 56,57 A retrospective study looking at surgery in patients who were treated with dabrafenib and trametinib 6 checkpoint in- hibitor therapy indicates that patients with BRAF V600E mutation–positive ATC who are treated with upfront neo- adjuvant dabrafenib and trametinib 6 immune checkpoint inhibitor followed by surgery have the longest survival when compared to those who had upfront surgery or no surgery. 58 There are inherent biases of such a study due to the retro- spective nature. A prospective study with neoadjuvant dabrafenib, trametinib, and pembrolizumab has been completed but is not yet published (ClinicalTrials.gov identiﬁer: NCT04675710). Clinical interpretation. These results support the use of BRAF V600E–targeted therapy in patients with BRAF V600E mutation–positive ATC. However, the true median OS re- sults of the prospective trial of dabrafenib and trametinib alone should be interpreted with caution.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Since patients who responded were able to proceed to surgical resection or radiation, the reported median OS might overestimate the true survival beneﬁt attributable to the drugs alone, as the cure or control achieved by subsequent local therapy likely contributed signiﬁcantly to the extended survival. Given this context, the use of these drugs as neoadjuvant therapy followed by surgery or radiotherapy may be the most impactful. Recommendation 10.1.1 Literature review and analysis. The only trial to com- pare patients treated with BRAF/MEK inhibitor (dabrafenib 1 trametinib) to BRAF/MEK inhibitor 1 immune checkpoint inhibitor (dabrafenib 1 trametinib 1 pembrolizumab) was a nonrandomized, retrospective study. 59 The primary analysis included 71 patients; 34 treated with dabrafenib 1 trametinib 1 pembrolizumab and 14 also received pembrolizumab in addition to dabrafenib 1 trametinib at disease progression (total n 5 48). There were 23 patients in the dabrafenib 1 trametinib alone group.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: The median OS of patients in the upfront dabrafenib 1 trametinib 1 pembrolizumab or the addition of pembrolizumab to dabrafenib 1 trametinib at disease progression was 17 months, and 9 months in the dabrafenib 1 trametinib alone group. An exploratory group of an additional 23 patients who underwent surgery after upfront dabrafenib 1 trametinib 1 pembrolizumab had a median OS of 63 months. A prospective, nonrandomized trial included 19 patients treated with BRAF or MEK inhibitor 1 anti–PD-L1 drugs. 51 The median PFS and OS were 13.9 and 43 months, respectively. Patients were permitted to undergo surgery during the trial. Both trials included patients with stage IVB and IVC diseases. It should be noted that patients who underwent surgical resection after BRAF or MEK in- hibitor 1 immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy resumed these drugs shortly after surgery. Patients with stage IVB disease typically underwent chemoradiation after surgical resection and then continued BRAF or MEK inhibitor 1 immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy. Clinical interpretation.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Patients with stage IVB and IVC BRAF V600E mutation–positive ATC should be considered for upfront dabrafenib and trametinib 1 pembrolizumab to rapidly control the disease, reduce tumor bulk, and, cru- cially, convert initially unresectable or borderline-resectable disease into a surgically resectable state. After a favorable response, surgical resection may be considered with a multidisciplinary team to assess the extent of response and surgical feasibility. 1362 | © 2026 by American Society of Clinical Oncology Saba et al Downloaded from ascopubs.org by 181.223.170.21 on October 23, 2026 from 181.223.170.021 Copyright © 2026 American Society of Clinical Oncology. chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Recommendation 10.2 Literature review and analysis. Larotrectinib and entrectinib are both FDA-approved for treating solid tumors with NTRK fusions in both adult and pediatric patients. In the seven patients with ATC from a pooled analysis of three single-arm trials with larotrectinib, the ORR was 29% (95% CI, 4 to 71), with two partial responses, with 50% main- taining the response at 12 months. 74 One additional patient had stable disease, and both the 12- and 24-month PFS was 17%, with an OS at those time points of 50% and 17%, re- spectively. Four out of seven patients had not received prior systemic therapy, and three had received one line of prior therapy, which was with chemotherapy. In a retrospective study of 65 patients with NTRK fusion–positive thyroid cancer, two of four patients with ATC had a partial response to therapy. 86 Selpercatinib is FDA approved for RET fusion–positive thyroid cancer and RET mutation–positive MTC. Two pa- tients with ATC were included in the Libretto-001 pro- spective study, with one patient reported having a partial response that lasted for 18 months. 26 Clinical interpretation.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Given the extremely poor prog- nosis of ATC and limited prospective data, the existing FDA approvals for these agents in tumors harboring the re- spective fusions the substantial and durable response rates observed with NTRK inhibitors (eg, larotrectinib, entrecti- nib) and RET inhibitors (eg, selpercatinib, pralsetinib) in other advanced thyroid and solid tumors provide strong justiﬁcation for their use in this setting while awaiting more extensive ATC-speciﬁc clinical trial data. Recommendation 10.3 Literature review and analysis. There is no published literature evaluating subsequent-line therapy after disease progression on genomically targeted therapy. Given the poor outcomes of these patients, participation in clinical trials is recommended. However, prospective evaluation demon- strates a low response rate in ATC without a genomic mu- tation managed with lenvatinib alone or lenvatinib with pembrolizumab, and may be offered as an established, broad-spectrum, second-line systemic option when speciﬁc targeted salvage therapies or clinical trials are unavailable. Clinical interpretation.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Clinical trials, when available or feasible, should be considered in patients who have disease progression on genomically targeted therapy. If these are not available [NA], lenvatinib 6 pembrolizumab may be considered. Question 11 In patients with ATC, does immunotherapy impact response and/or survival and what should be recommended in the ﬁrst-line and subsequent-line setting? Recommendation 11.1 Literature review and analysis. There are two studies showing efﬁcacy of the combination therapies, lenvatinib 1 pembrolizumab or ipilimumab 1 nivolumab, for treatment of advanced ATC without a genomic mutation in ﬁrst-line setting. One prospective, single-arm, phase II clinical trial using lenvatinib in combination with pembrolizumab in non–BRAF V600E mutation–positive ATC with 25 patients were studied, of which 96% had upfront treatment to the primary tumor prior to study entry. The primary end point was median OS compared to 3-month OS from the single- agent lenvatinib clinical trial with the goal of improving survival by 3 months. 62 The median OS in the combination trial was 11.4 months, thus meeting the study end point (95% CI, 7.8 to 35.6; P < .025).

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: The best overall response in target lesions was 36%. Bleeding and ﬁstula were rare but serious events that merit caution in patients at risk for these complications. Another study with ipilimumab 1 nivolumab 5 included differentiated thyroid cancers, including MTC and ATC. This was a phase II nonrandomized trial of intravenous nivolumab (3 mg/kg) once every 2 weeks and ipilimumab (1 mg/kg) once every 6 weeks. Treatment was continued until disease progression or intolerable side effects, or maximum time of 2 years. 10 patients with ATC were included in this study. 90% of patients had prior surgery for thyroid cancer, 80% had prior radiation therapy, and 70% had received prior systemic therapy. Eight patients discontinued treatment because of disease progression (n 5 4), adverse effects (n 5 3), or withdrew consent (n 5 1). Two patients completed the entire 2 years of treatment. Three of the 10 patients achieved partial response with ORR of 30% (95% CI, 6.7% to 65.2%). The median PFS was 4.3 months (95% CI, 0.5 to NA). The 12-and 24-month OS rates were 55.6% (95% CI, 20.4% to 80.5%). The observed ORR was 30% and 50%, which is favorable in comparison to anti–PD-1 monotherapy.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Clinical interpretation. For patients with advanced ATC without a genomic mutation, treatment selection is chal- lenging due to the limited efﬁcacy of historical options and the aggressive nature of the disease. The combination of lenvatinib 1 pembrolizumab or the dual immune checkpoint blockade of ipilimumab 1 nivolumab may be offered as systemic therapeutic options. Despite the availability of these systemic options, ATC carries an extremely high risk of local complications (eg, airway compression, bleeding, dysphagia). Therefore, upfront palliation and control of the primary tumor should be the immediate priority. Recommendation 11.2 Literature review and analysis. The only trial to examine the addition of pembrolizumab to dabrafenib plus trametinib after disease progression with dabrafenib plus trametinib alone was a retrospective study of 71 patients with BRAF mutation–positive ATC.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: pembrolizumab added to the regimen. The median OS of these patients was 16 months (95% CI, 6.4 to 25.6). 59 Clinical interpretation. While the retrospective nature and small cohort size of this study limit the strength of the evidence, the observed median OS of 16 months following the addition of pembrolizumab to dabrafenib plus trametinib in patients whose disease progressed on the dual therapy alone suggests a clinically meaningful beneﬁt in the highly ag- gressive, BRAF mutation–positive ATC setting. Pending prospective data, this triplet regimen may be considered as a salvage option for patients who have disease progression on BRAF or MEK inhibitors. For patients with stage IVB disease who have completed upfront multimodal treatment (surgery when feasible 1 radiation with radiosensitizing chemotherapy), adjuvant treatment with pembrolizumab for 2 years may be consid- ered, starting 4-6 weeks after completion of radiation.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: A cohort study of patients with stage IVB (locoregional disease; N 5 16) used a pooled analysis of prospective and retro- spective patients treated with adjuvant pembrolizumab after upfront surgery (when feasible) and chemoradiation com- pared to age- and treatment-matched historical controls who did not receive adjuvant pembrolizumab. 87 The median PFS was not reached in the adjuvant pembrolizumab arm and was 5.4 months in the control arm (95% CI, 2.04 to 16.20; P 5 .006; HR, 0.24 [95% CI, 0.08 to 0.73]). The median OS was not reached in the adjuvant pembrolizumab group and was 31 months in the control arm (95% CI, 13.9 to NA; P 5 .009; HR, 0.11 [95% CI, 0.01 to 0.83]). Immune-related adverse events included grade 2 pneumonitis. One other patient had gastric ischemia leading to sepsis and death, but it was unclear if related to pembrolizumab since the patient was on treatment for chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Thus, patients with stage IVB ATC who complete surgery (when feasible) and deﬁnitive radiation (6radiosensitizing chemotherapy) may be considered for adjuvant pembrolizumab. However, patients should be made aware of potential immune-related adverse events.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Question 12 In patients with ATC, does cytotoxic chemotherapy com- pared to targeted agents or MKIs impact response and/or survival and what should be recommended in the ﬁrst-line and subsequent-line setting? Recommendation 12.1 Literature review and analysis. No comparative trials of targeted therapy and cytotoxic chemotherapy have been completed in ATC, and studies utilizing cytotoxic chemo- therapy in ATC predate the use of targeted therapy. Due to time delay from ordering to receiving molecular testing, in a retrospective trial of 16 patients with ATC, ﬁve patients received “bridging” chemotherapy with weekly nab- paclitaxel or paclitaxel, and one patient received carbopla- tin and paclitaxel until return of molecular testing and initiation of molecularly focused therapy. Time on bridging therapy was between 1 and 8 weeks, and none of the patients had disease progression while on bridging cytotoxic chemotherapy. 48 Clinical interpretation. There is no evidence to support the use of cytotoxic chemotherapy in patients who are candidates for genomically targeted therapies or MKIs.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: However, despite the limited data, in instances where mo- lecular data are not available or there is rapidly progressive disease, clinicians may offer cytotoxic chemotherapy. Recommendation 12.2 Literature review and analysis. The FACT trial 47 in- vestigated the role of adding the vascular disrupting agent fosbretabulin to standard chemotherapy (carboplatin and paclitaxel) in 80 patients with advanced thyroid cancer, and reported a nonsigniﬁcant difference in response rate, at 20% and 16%, respectively, and no complete responses. Fur- thermore, there was a nonsigniﬁcant difference in OS with fosbretabulin (5.2 v 4 months). However, it is important to note that none of the patients in this trial had received prior targeted therapy. A small retrospective series examined the use of carboplatin and pemetrexed in 14 patients, including 11 with refractory differentiated thyroid cancer and 3 with ATC. All three pa- tients with ATC had received prior immunotherapy and MKI. One patient, who also harbored a BRAF V600E mutation, did respond to carboplatin and pemetrexed that was sustained beyond 13 months. 49 Clinical interpretation.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: There are limited data supporting cytotoxic chemotherapy in ATC. Therefore, clinical trial enrollment is favored and strongly encouraged for patients who fail targeted therapy or MKIs. In the absence of clinical trials, cytotoxic chemotherapy can be considered. There is no favored cytotoxic chemotherapeutic agent, and combination chemotherapy has not been proven to be better than single- agent chemotherapy and decisions. MEDULLARY (MTC) The primary treatment of MTC is surgery. The following recommendations pertain to recurrent or metastatic disease after primary treatment. chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Recommendation 13.1 Literature review and analysis. Three RCTs investigated a MKI compared to placebo in patients with unresectable locally advanced and/or metastatic MTC. 32-34 ZETA was a phase III trial randomizing 331 patients to vandetanib or placebo in a 2:1 ratio, with a primary objective of PFS. 34 Progressive disease was not a requirement for trial entry. At disease progression, patients were unblinded, and those on placebo were offered vandetanib. The predicted median PFS with vandetanib was 30.5 versus 19.3 months with placebo (HR, 0.46; 95% CI, 0.31 to 0.69; P < .001). The ORR per RECIST with vandetanib was 45%. Responses were seen in RET mutation–positive, –negative, and –unknown pa- tients. OS data were immature at cutoff, but post hoc analysis of 184 ZETA patients with symptomatic and progressive disease at baseline showed no OS difference between the two groups. Adverse events led to treatment discontinuation in 12% of patients on the vandetanib arm. The phase III trial, EXAM, randomly assigned 330 patients with disease pro- gression within the prior 14 months to cabozantinib or placebo in a 2:1 ratio, with a primary objective of PFS.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: 32 Crossover to open-label cabozantinib at disease progres- sion in patients on placebo was not allowed. Median PFS with cabozantinib was 11.2 versus 4.0 months with placebo (HR, 0.28 [95% CI, 0.19 to 0.40]; P < .001). A PFS beneﬁt was seen across subgroups, including patients who had received a prior MKI and in RET mutation–positive, –negative, and –unknown patients. The ORR with cabozantinib was 28%. Median OS with cabozantinib versus placebo was 26.6 versus 21.1 months, which did not reach statistical signiﬁcance (stratiﬁed HR, 0.85 [95% CI, 0.64 to 1.12]; P 5 .24). Adverse events led to treatment discontinuation in 16% on the cabozantinib arm. Anlotinib was studied in a phase IIB trial randomizing 91 patients with MTC to anlotinib versus pla- cebo in a 2:1 ratio, with a primary objective of PFS. 33 At disease progression, patients were unblinded, and those on placebo were offered anlotinib. Median PFS with anlotinib was 20.7 months versus 11.1 months with placebo (HR, 0.53 [95% CI, 0.30 to 0.95]; P 5 .029). ORR with anlotinib was 48.4%. Follow-up for OS is ongoing. Adverse events led to treatment discontinuation in 16.1% of patients on anlotinib.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: This drug is approved in China and not available in the United States. Clinical interpretation. In patients with locally advanced and/or metastatic MTC, three MKIs, namely cabozantinib, vandetanib, and anlotinib (approved in China), demon- strated signiﬁcantly improved PFS compared to placebo in RCTs. These studies predated the phase III LIBRETTO-531 study discussed subsequently, and enrolled patients re- gardless of RET mutation status. 21 However, given the su- perior efﬁcacy and tolerability of selpercatinib in RET mutation–positive MTC, as shown in LIBRETTO-531, the recommendation for MKIs in the ﬁrst-line treatment of patients with MTC is limited to patients with RET wild-type disease. There is no head-to-head comparison of MKIs in MTC, and cross-trial comparisons are limited due to differences in study design and patient populations. Therefore, the choice of ﬁrst-line MKI should be made on a case-by-case basis. Recommendation 13.2 Literature review and analysis. Enrollment in the ZETA trial was limited to patients who were treatment-na ¨ ıve.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: 34 However, real-world analysis of 48 patients with locally advanced and/or distant metastatic MTC who were treated with vandetanib and/or cabozantinib revealed second-line vandetanib following ﬁrst-line cabozantinib may result in partial responses, as can second-line cabozantinib following ﬁrst-line vandetanib. 42 EXAM did allow prior MKI treatment. Twenty-one percent of patients received a prior MKI, in- cluding vandetanib and sorafenib, and the prespeciﬁed subgroup analysis conﬁrmed a signiﬁcant PFS beneﬁt i n these patients. Clinical interpretation. In patients with RET wild-type recurrent or metastatic MTC who have received prior MKI therapy, the limited available data regarding second-line treatment or beyond suggest that patients can derive clin- ical beneﬁt from MKI treatment beyond the ﬁrst-line set- ting, with the best evidence available supporting vandetanib in patients who had disease progression on cabozantinib or vice versa. 32,42 Question 14 In patients with MTC, do genomically targeted therapies compared to placebo or observation impact survival and what is recommended in the ﬁrst-line setting and subsequent-line setting?

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Recommendation 14.1 Literature review and analysis. Two RET kinase–spe- ciﬁc inhibitors were studied in the phase I/II setting in patients with RET mutation–positive locally advanced and/ or metastatic MTC, either with or without prior MKI treatment, namely selpercatinib and pralsetinib. 25,26 Both RET-speciﬁc therapies demonstrated high ORRs, long me- dian PFS, and a well-tolerated safety proﬁle in patients who were previously treated and treatment-na ¨ ıve. Selpercatinib was subsequently studied in LIBRETTO-531, a phase III RCT comparing selpercatinib to physician’s choice (cabozantinib or vandetanib) in 291 patients with treatment-na ¨ ıve, RET mutation–positive, locally advanced and/or metastatic MTC who had disease progression within 14 months from en- rollment. 21 Patients were allocated 2:1 to selpercatinib versus the control arm, and followed for PFS as the study’s primary end point. Crossover to open-label selpercatinib with disease progression in patients on the control arm was allowed. Median PFS with selpercatinib was not reached versus 16.8 months in the control group (HR, 0.28 [95% CI, 0.16 to 0.48]; P < .001).

chunks.text: discontinuation of treatment due to treatment-related ad- verse events, or death, was a key secondary end point considered a composite measure of treatment-related ef- ﬁcacy and tolerability, and it was signiﬁcantly improved with selpercatinib versus control. At a median follow-up of 15 months, a total of 18 deaths had occurred. The observed HR for death from any cause was 0.37 (95% CI, 0.15 to 0.95). Pralsetinib was not studied in the phase III setting, despite the promising phase I/II results. Clinical interpretation. Selpercatinib is considered the preferred ﬁrst-line therapy for progressive RET mutation– positive unresectable locally advanced and/or metastatic MTC based on safety and efﬁcacy outcomes from LIBRETTO- 531. Long-term follow-up data from the phase I/II selper- catinib study, LIBRETTO-001, support this, showing a higher ORR and longer median PFS in patients who were treatment-na ¨ ıve compared to patients previously treated with an MKI. 27 Of note, RET-speciﬁc inhibitors have dem- onstrated similar activity and safety proﬁles in patients with hereditary MTC harboring germline RET mutations. 28 Recommendation 14.2 Literature review and analysis.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Clinical trials investi- gating new treatment strategies in patients with RET mutation–positive MTC with disease progression on a RET- speciﬁc inhibitor such as selpercatinib or pralsetinib have not yet been conducted. In the largest series of the devel- opment of resistance to RET-speciﬁc inhibitors in RET mutation–positive MTC available to date, both on-target RET mutations and bypass pathway acquired resistance al- terations were found, sometimes polyclonal, on molecular proﬁling of progressive disease. 29 Response to subsequent lines of therapy was not reported. Clinical interpretation. The mechanisms of acquired resistance to RET-speciﬁc inhibitor therapy in patients with RET mutation–positive MTC are diverse and often poly- clonal, with both on-target and bypass pathway resistance emerging. This is a major clinical challenge necessitating the study of new approaches for this patient population. Question 15 In patients with MTC, does immunotherapy compared to targeted agents or MKIs impact response and/or survival and what is recommended in the ﬁrst-line and subsequent-line setting? Recommendation 15.1 Literature review and analysis.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Although several reg- istered trials have explored the potential efﬁcacy of im- munotherapy in MTC, limited published studies have not convincingly demonstrated efﬁcacy. In a phase II non- randomized trial, the efﬁcacy of dual immune checkpoint inhibition (nivolumab and ipilimumab) was explored in seven patients with MTC. No responses were observed in this exploratory cohort. Of the seven patients with MTC, two patients had stable disease, with a clinical beneﬁt rate of 28.6%. 5 An open-label, nonrandomized, single-center phase II trial of pembrolizumab in recurrent or metastatic MTC enrolled patients with recurrent or metastatic MTC in one of two arms: pembrolizumab with or without an immune-stimulating cancer vaccine. 88 Only two patients from the vaccine group completed the study, and none of the patients enrolled achieved a response. Clinical interpretation. Considering the unsatisfactory activity of immunotherapy and no head-to-head trials comparing immunotherapy to targeted agents or MKIs, clinicians should not offer immunotherapy in the ﬁrst-line setting or when other treatment is available in subsequent lines, outside of participation in clinical trials.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Question 16 In patients with MTC, does cytotoxic chemotherapy com- pared to targeted agents or MKIs impact response and/or survival and what is recommended in the ﬁrst-line and subsequent-line setting? Recommendation 16.1 Literature review and analysis. Cytotoxic chemotherapy has been evaluated in small clinical series of patients with MTC from the 1970s through the 1990s, with agents such as doxorubicin, dacarbazine, streptozocin, cyclophosphamide, and 5-ﬂuorouracil. These studies consistently demonstrated the limited efﬁcacy of cytotoxic chemotherapy in patients with progressive or recurrent MTC. Objective responses were low and usually partial, and short-lived. Median PFS was <6 months, complete responses were exceedingly rare, and there was no proven survival beneﬁt. 89,90 In a single-arm GETC study (N 5 20), alternating 5-ﬂuorouracil plus streptozocin with 5-ﬂuorouracil plus dacarbazine produced three partial responses and 11 long-term stabilizations; no PFS or survival advantage was demonstrated.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: 89 In a second GETC series (N 5 20), alternating doxorubicin plus strep- tozocin with 5-ﬂuorouracil plus dacarbazine reported three partial responses and 10 stabilizations, without time-to- event efﬁcacy. 90 These historical outcomes are in stark contrast to the targeted agents. Moreover, cytotoxic regi- mens are associated with signiﬁcant toxicities, including myelosuppression, GI intolerance, and cardiotoxicity, which limited their tolerability in most patients. Clinical interpretation. Due to poor efﬁcacy and high toxicity with cytotoxic chemotherapy, clinicians should not offer cytotoxic chemotherapy in the ﬁrst-line setting out- side of a clinical trial. Recommendation 16.2 Literature review and analysis. In patients with pro- gressive or recurrent MTC after ﬁrst-line therapy, con- ventional cytotoxic chemotherapy shows modest and short- 1366 | © 2026 by American Society of Clinical Oncology Saba et al Downloaded from ascopubs.org by 181.223.170.21 on October 23, 2026 from 181.223.170.021 Copyright © 2026 American Society of Clinical Oncology. All rights reserved.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: lived efﬁcacy, with historical series reporting low ORRs and limited disease control despite multiagent regimens alternat- ing 5-ﬂuorouracil plus streptozocin with 5-ﬂuorouracil plus dacarbazine. These data did not demonstrate a reproducible survival advantage and were accompanied by substantial toxicity, which becomes even less acceptable as patients accumulate prior therapies. 91 Current expert guidelines also reﬂect this, characterizing cytotoxic chemotherapy as having a minor or limited role in metastatic MTC and recommend prioritizing other therapies, reserving cyto- toxic chemotherapy for situations where targeted options and clinical trials are exhausted or unsuitable. 92 Clinical interpretation. After disease progression on initial therapy, patients derive limited beneﬁt from cytotoxic chemotherapy. The poor efﬁcacy and higher toxicity of cytotoxic chemotherapy in this setting provide a clear clinical rationale to avoid it outside a trial. LIMITATION OF RESEARCH AND FUTURE RESEARCH Thyroid cancer comprises a diverse set of diseases with sub- stantial variation in expected outcomes and optimal treat- ments.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: In the last decades, paradigm shifts in the diagnosis and characterization of thyroid cancers, including changes in the WHO classiﬁcation and increasing importance of molec- ular descriptions, have further impacted the optimal therapies for patients affected by these malignancies. The recommen- dations included are based on analysis of existing literature and clinical trials, which are affected by these changes as well as the rarity of some of these diagnoses (such as ATC). In each case, the recommendations have been informed by the best available data. For well-differentiated and medullary cancers, there are several studies to reference for treatment recom- mendations. For differentiated high-grade or PDTC and an- aplastic cancers, many recommendations are based on extrapolation due to the type of data available in these diseases. Regarding differentiated high-grade or PDTC tumors, this characterization was noted in the WHO 2022 update to pa- thology of thyroid malignancies. As such, it has not been robustly integrated into prior trials.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: There are several trials of well-differentiated thyroid carcinomas that include this subtype (or its pathological predecessors) and as well several studies of anaplastic thyroid carcinomas that include this subtype (or its pathological predecessors). In these cases, the numbers are limited. Therefore, the overall recommendations are limited, with note of potential acceptable approaches to systemic therapy based on extrapolation. Similarly, for anaplastic thyroid carcinomas, there have been profound changes in the approach to these malignancies due to newer molecular characterization and integration of systemic therapy into the multidisciplinary evaluation of these patients. However, due to the rarity of the cancer and its propensity to progress rapidly, randomized trials are limited and the numbers of patients included on trials are also small. The recommendations represent the synthesis of several studies; however, many are based on smaller patient populations, given the disease itself.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Overall, the advances in the treatment of thyroid carcinomas (of all types) have led to improvements over prior ap- proaches, especially with the integration of systemic therapy into multidisciplinary evaluation. There is a signiﬁcant opportunity to augment the quality of data available and, more importantly, provide patients with novel therapeutic approaches through clinical trials. PATIENT AND CLINICIAN COMMUNICATION Clinician and patient communication is extremely important, because of the multiple clinical issues that will likely occur over time. A well-organized, cohesive interprofessional practice approach brings additional, strategic value to this dynamic as well. Patients will typically interact with a variety of clinical personnel over many years. The oncology team should orient patients and their caregivers regarding achieving consistent care and set expectations for long-term follow-up. Care should be given to not overwhelm the patient and caregiver and, if necessary, short-term goals (ie, ﬁrst follow up) can be prioritized over the “big picture” if nec- essary.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Patients should be offered every available resource for short- and long-term support and encouraged to explore independent support services (ThyCa, etc) if desired. Keeping engaged in an active follow-up plan can keep patients aware of any advances in treatment paradigms and the optimal outcome if their disease recurs through timely intervention. Additionally, patients often experience distress about the “right questions” to ask their health care team. In practice, it may be of comfort to mention that physicians and providers are generally expected to proactively educate patients with all relevant information regardless of whether or not they are speciﬁcally asked by patients. However, patients should feel empowered to ask any and all questions that are meaningful to them. Patient and clinician communication is a dynamic rela- tionship that evolves over time and beneﬁts from clear communication and trust on both sides. This goal of an effective working relationship may be best achieved by empowering both clinicians and patients to work together to advocate for the best outcome for the patient in ways out- lined in this section.

In the United States, many patients remain unable to reap the beneﬁts of innovative prevention and early detection programs, biomarker testing, and new cancer therapies due to challenges including lack of transportation, stable housing, adequate insurance coverage, food insecurity, health literacy, proximity to a dedicated cancer center, and cost of treatment and other services. 94 Additionally, some populations experience stigma along with barriers to cancer screening, prevention, and treatment that contribute to these cancer disparities. 95 Further, geographic disparities can also impact the quality- of-care patients receive. Rural patients are more likely to have worse survivorship outcomes and experience higher mortality rates compared to nonrural patients. This can be attributed, in part, to a lower density of specialists and dedicated cancer centers, as only 21% of nonmetropolitan counties in the United States have one or more practicing oncologists.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: 96 In 2025, ASCO updated its guideline protocol template to include a patient access considerations section, allowing the Panel to consider patient access issues prior to starting the literature search. Patients of all ages, socioeconomic statuses, education levels, and locations may be affected by thyroid carcinoma. At all stages, access to knowledgeable multidisciplinary profes- sionals that understand the importance of coordinated care is crucial to outcomes. This is especially true for recurrent diseases, metastatic disease, and rare cancer entities (such as anaplastic thyroid carcinoma). Not all patients have consistent access to the resources needed to beneﬁt from ASCO’s expert recommendations on the treatment of thyroid cancer; access to diagnostic testing and multidisciplinary treatment (including surgery, nuclear medicine, radiation oncology, endocrinology, and medical oncology teams) is not consistent throughout the nation, especially in areas that are underserved. For thyroid carcinoma, pathologic interpretation and mo- lecular testing are necessary to characterize the disease and optimize the treatment plan.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Furthermore, access to the necessary systemic therapy medications, including MKIs, may vary based on treatment location. Finally, many thyroid malignancies are rare; expertise in management is not universal and may impact care. Overall, there is signiﬁcant opportunity to improve access to swift diagnosis, high-quality pathological diagnosis, and expertise in multidisciplinary treatment of thyroid carci- nomas to improve patient care. MULTIPLE CHRONIC CONDITIONS Creating evidence-based recommendations to inform treat- ment of patients with additional chronic conditions, a situa- tion in which the patient may have two or more such conditions—referred to as multiple chronic conditions (MCC)—is challenging. Patients with MCC are a complex and heterogeneous population, making it difﬁcult to account for all of the possible permutations to develop speciﬁc recommen- dations for care. In addition, the best available evidence for treating index conditions, such as cancer, is often from clinical trials whose study selection criteria may exclude these patients in order to avoid potential interaction effects or confounding of results associated with MCC.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: As a result, the reliability of outcome data from these studies may be limited, thereby creating constraints for expert groups to make recommen- dations for care in this heterogeneous patient population. As many patients for whom guideline recommendations apply present with MCC, any treatment plan needs to consider the complexity and uncertainty created by the presence of MCC and highlight the importance of shared decision making re- garding guideline use and implementation. Therefore, in consideration of recommended care for the target index condition, clinicians should review all other chronic condi- tions present in the patient and take those conditions into account when formulating the treatment and follow-up plan. In light of these considerations, practice guidelines should provide information on how to apply the recommendations for patients with MCC, perhaps as a qualifying statement for recommended care. This may mean that some or all of the recommended care options are modiﬁed or not applied, as determined by best practice in consideration of any MCC.

chunks.text: and coinsurance. 97,98 Higher patient out-of-pocket costs have been shown to be a barrier to initiating and adhering to recommended cancer treatments. 99,100 Discussion of cost can be an important part of shared de- cision making. 101 Clinicians should discuss with patients the use of less expensive alternatives when it is practical and feasible for treatment of the patient’s disease and there are two or more treatment options that are comparable in terms of beneﬁts and harms. 101 Patient out-of-pocket costs may vary depending on insur- ance coverage. Coverage may originate in the medical or pharmacy beneﬁt, which may have different cost-sharing arrangements. Patients should be aware that different products may be preferred or covered by their particular insurance plan. Even with the same insurance plan, the price may vary between different pharmacies. When discussing ﬁnancial issues and concerns, patients should be made aware of any ﬁnancial counseling services available to address this complex and heterogeneous landscape.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: 101 As part of the guideline development process, ASCO may opt to search the literature for published cost-effectiveness analyses that might inform the relative value of available treatment options. Excluded from consideration are cost- effectiveness analyses that lack contemporary cost data; agents that are not currently available in either the United States or Canada; or are industry-sponsored. Four cost-effectiveness analysis were identiﬁed to inform the topic. 102-105 The publication dates of these evaluations ranged from 2013 to 2019. While earlier evaluations 102 highlighted a foundational lack of economic data in RAI-refractory, dif- ferentiated thyroid cancer, subsequent modeling has yielded inconsistent results regarding the incremental cost- effectiveness ratio for agents like lenvatinib and sorafenib.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Speciﬁcally, a 2017 analysis found lenvatinib to be cost- effective within a US context, 103 yet a comprehensive UK evaluation 104 published in 2020 determined that neither lenvatinib nor sorafenib met the acceptable willingness-to- Pay (WTP) threshold for the UK National Health Service; similar issues of ICERs exceeding acceptable thresholds were identiﬁed for targeted agents, cabozantinib and vandetanib, in MTC. 105 GUIDELINE IMPLEMENTATION ASCO guidelines are developed for implementation across health settings. Each ASCO guideline includes a community oncologist member on the panel. The additional role of this community oncologist member on the guideline panel is not only to assess the suitability of the recommendations for implementation in the community setting, but also to identify any other barrier to implementation a reader should be aware of. Barriers to implementation include the need to increase awareness of the guideline recommendations among frontline practitioners and survivors of cancer and caregivers, and also to provide adequate services in the face of limited resources.

chunks.text: APPENDIX 1. GUIDELINE DISCLAIMER The Clinical Practice Guidelines and other guidance published herein are provided by the ASCO, Inc to assist clinicians in clinical decision making. The information herein should not be relied upon as being complete or accurate, nor should it be considered as inclusive of all proper treatments or methods of care or as a statement of the standard of care. With the rapid development of scientiﬁc knowledge, new evidence may emerge between the time information is developed and when it is published or read. The information is not continually updated and may not reﬂect the most recent evidence. The information addresses only the topics speciﬁcally identiﬁed therein and is not applicable to other interventions, diseases, or stages of diseases. This in- formation does not mandate any particular course of medical care. Further, the information is not intended to substitute for the independent professional judgment of the treating clinician, as the information does not account for individual variation among patients. Recommendations specify the level of conﬁdence that the rec- ommendation reﬂects the net effect of a given course of action.

All members of the Expert Panel completed ASCO’s disclosure form, which requires disclosure of ﬁnancial and other interests, including relationships with commercial entities that are reasonably likely to ex- perience direct regulatory or commercial impact as a result of promulgation of the guideline. Categories for disclosure include employment; leadership; stock or other ownership; honoraria, consulting, or advisory role; speaker’s bureau; research funding; patents, royalties, other intellectual property; expert testimony; travel, ac- commodations, expenses; and other relationships. In accordance with the Policy, the majority of the members of the Expert Panel did not disclose any relationships constituting a conﬂict under the Policy.

chunks.title: ASCO systemic treatment of thyroid cancer guideline
chunks.text: Moderate We are moderately conﬁdent in the effect estimate: The true effect is likely to be close to the estimate of the effect, but there is a possibility that it is substantially different. Low Our conﬁdence in the effect estimate is limited: The true effect may be sub- stantially different from the estimate of the effect. Very low We have very little conﬁdence in the effect estimate: The true effect is likely to be substantially different from the estimate of effect. Strength of recommendation Strong In recommendations for an intervention, the desirable effects of an intervention outweigh its undesirable effects. In recommendations against an intervention, the undesirable effects of an intervention outweigh its desirable effects. All or almost all informed people would make the recommended choice for or against an intervention. Conditional In recommendations for an intervention, the desirable effects probably outweigh the undesirable effects, but appreciable uncertainty exists. In recommendations against an intervention, the undesirable effects probably outweigh the desirable effects, but appreciable uncertainty exists.
